items.title: From Vision to Interaction: Evaluating Dynamic Social Intelligence of VLM Agents in ALIVE-World
items.abstract: As AI agents are increasingly deployed in real-world applications and take on social roles, dynamic social intelligence, the ability to continuously perceive multimodal cues, infer latent cognitive states, intervene through embodied actions, and ultimately achieve social goals, has become essential. However, existing evaluations largely fragment social intelligence into text-based abstractions, static reasoning tasks, or embodied simulators that lack social dynamics. These approaches fail to capture the multimodal, continuous, and interpersonal complexity of authentic human interactions. To bridge this gap, we introduce ALIVE-World, an embodied simulation environment supporting dynamic multimodal interactions encompassing egocentric vision, language, and non-verbal action. To provide socially grounded interactive feedback, we populate this environment with counterpart agents driven by a profile-conditioned, dual-system (intuitive-affective and logical-cognitive) architecture. Building upon this platform, we propose ALIVE-Bench to transform the assessment of social intelligence into a trackable quantitative framework. By deeply leveraging underlying environmental states and agents' internal variables, ALIVE-Bench systematically evaluates Vision-Language Model (VLM) agents across four critical dimensions: perception, understanding, influence, and outcome. Extensive evaluations reveal that dynamic social intelligence is fundamentally multi-dimensional and scenario-dependent. We identify a critical bottleneck between upstream perception and downstream social intervention, exposing VLM vulnerabilities in fine-grained proxemic awareness, adaptive intervention, and multi-party coordination. By uncovering these limitations and the diverse interaction strategies they produce, this benchmark provides actionable insights for the future behavioral alignment of multimodal agents.

items.title: Gamified Resistance and the Reproduction of Platform Control: Jiacan in China's Food‐Delivery Sector
items.abstract: This article examines Jiacan, Chinese food‐delivery riders' term for retaining or consuming undelivered food. Drawing on digital ethnography of rider chat groups, interviews, Douyin vlogs and public discussion threads, it shows how grievance‐linked Jiacan acquires resistant meaning through customer‐mediated disputes, digital circulation and peer evaluation. We develop Gamified Resistance to describe resistance socially organised through shared procedures, risk–reward calculations and judgments about acceptable conduct. The analysis identifies three pathways through which resistance may reproduce platform control: proceduralised rule‐navigation, triadic displacement toward customers and priced dissent. Riders can obtain immediate relief or retaliation while sustaining dependence on platform adjudication, customer‐mediated relations and sanctions. Control reproduction remains provisional: peer judgments, public scrutiny and customer claims can regulate participation and channel disputes, but also challenge the practice or redirect conflict toward the platform.

items.title: Generative AI and the Crisis of Higher Education Assessments: Examining 'AI-Proofing' Strategies for College-Level Assessments
items.abstract: Higher education is confronting an academic-integrity challenge unlike any in its history. Students can now outsource homework, take-home assignments, and online examinations to large language models (LLMs) that complete them in seconds. Existing research on evaluating LLM performance on academic assessments has focused largely on standardized examinations, or on questions from college-level courses drawn from a single discipline. Far less is known about how LLMs perform on college-level assessment questions spanning multiple disciplines, that instructors have purposely designed to be AI-resistant, and about which features of such questions, if any, meaningfully constrain LLM performance. We address this gap by collecting 75 questions from authentic college coursework assessments, spanning 17 disciplines, which were contributed by 37 faculty members from ten U.S. universities and one U.K. university. Of these, 61 questions were intentionally designed by faculty members to be 'LLM-proof', while the remaining 14 questions were sourced from online courses. We then (i) evaluate three state-of-the-art LLMs' ability to correctly answer these questions with and without supplementary course materials; (ii) identify five strategies, through thematic analysis, that faculty used to make their questions harder for LLMs to solve; and (iii) test whether these strategies impact LLMs' ability to answer the questions accurately. Our experimental results show that the best-performing model scored approximately 83% without supplementary course materials and 85% with them, and we observed noteworthy differences across models, answer formats, and instructor tweaking strategies. We discuss implications for assessment design, academic-integrity policy, and the broader ethics of deploying LLMs in educational settings.

items.title: Hivemind: A Federated Protocol for AI-Mediated Tacit Knowledge Sharing in Organisations
items.abstract: This paper presents Hivemind, a federated protocol that enables AI agents to exchange tacit knowledge on behalf of their users, asynchronously and without requiring any direct human interaction. Individual AI memory systems capture the decisions, reasoning, and contextual knowledge that surface during AI-assisted work. Hivemind creates the shared space in which this captured knowledge can flow between individuals across team and departmental boundaries, addressing a structural gap that neither centralised knowledge repositories nor existing AI tooling closes, even where partial solutions such as expert-finding systems exist. The paper evaluates centralised versus decentralised design approaches, proposes a federated architecture grounded in Nonaka and Takeuchi's (1995) Socialisation, Externalisation, Combination and Internalisation (SECI) model, and demonstrates a proof-of-concept implementation using Design Science Research (DSR) methodology. Measuring the enterprise benefit of federated tacit expertise sharing remains an open task for future work.

items.title: How Developer Personality Shapes the Use of AI Coding Assistants
items.abstract: Developers differ in personality traits that shape how they approach software development tasks, yet AI coding assistants either behave uniformly or offer personalization features whose fit with individual developers must be found through trial and error. This is because it remains unclear how personality shapes developers' experiences with AI assistants, and thus which traits personalization should account for. In other words, we provide tools with no underlying theory on what works when and why. We take a first step towards such a theory with a systematic scoping review on how users' personality relates to their perception of LLM-based tools. We identified twelve studies through general search engines, major Software Engineering (SE) venues, AI tooling, and snowballing. They all reported associations between personality and perceptions, particularly perceived usefulness, yet none addressed this in a SE context. Building on these findings, we conducted an exploratory two-wave survey with 29 and 11 developers, collecting first empirical evidence of how developers' personality (measured using the Big Five Model) relates to the perception of AI coding assistants. Higher Extraversion was associated with more positive private-use experiences in both waves, while Agreeableness was associated with negative professional experiences in the first wave and positive ones in the second. These results provide first indications that the personality effects found in the literature extend to developers. Although further studies with bigger samples are needed to build a theory, our work takes the first step towards an empirical grounded theory of developer personality and AI personalization traits.

items.title: How to Translate Ergonomics Findings into Design-Relevant Principles in an Ergodesign Framework: The Case of Lohr Industrie
items.abstract: Aligning human capabilities with system requirements is crucial for lowering injury risks and enhancing performance in industrial settings like the assembly of automobiles. In this context, we define the Ergodesign Framework as a structure for integrating ergonomics and its findings, Ergodesign and its generation of principles, and design and its pursuit of technical solutions within a transdisciplinary, continuous, and bidirectional process. In this paper, we focus on the internal Ergodesign process, whose objective is to translate ergonomic data into design-relevant principles that can subsequently be applied during design phases, thereby enabling the proactive implementation of ergonomic requirements. The process is based on the capitalization of recurring issues observed during ergonomic analyses, the identification of their root causes, and the definition of Ergodesign rules, making it possible to create a database of Ergodesign principles that can be applied by designers. This process is implemented within the company Lohr Industrie, where standardized elements were developed to define internal rules for product and process design, based on findings from ergonomic studies conducted across different workshops. Through this application, the process of translating ergonomic data into design-relevant principles via Ergodesign emerges as a central component of the Ergodesign Framework.

items.title: Human and Ethical Factors in AI- and IoT-Driven Industry 5.0 Smart Manufacturing: A PRISMA-Guided Systematic and Narrative Review
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) and the Internet of Things (IoT) are promoted as the technological backbone of Industry 5.0, which re-centres manufacturing on human well-being, resilience, and sustainability. This PRISMA 2020-guided review combines bibliometric analysis with narrative synthesis to examine how the human and ethical dimensions of AI- and IoT-driven smart manufacturing are addressed. Web of Science, Scopus, and IEEE Xplore searches without a start-year limit identified 1904 unique records; all were coded at abstract level (647 eligible records), and 86 prioritized records were synthesized in full text around five research questions: ethical risk, human factors, operationalization of human-centricity, governance, and the technology-readiness gap. Performance, thematic-evolution, co-citation, usage, and readership analyses complement the synthesis. Human-factors and architecture research dominate, yet reviews and conceptual papers prevail, and only 10% of eligible records report industrial validation. Ethical risk is the fastest-growing theme but is operationalized mainly as explainability. Governance is the primary object of 2.8% of eligible records, and its intellectual base is thin: about 3% of these studies cite the EU AI Act, the GDPR, or AI-law scholarship. A human-centric Industry 5.0 maturity model and a research agenda are proposed.

items.title: Human-AI Co-Ideation Across Socio-Technical Configurations: An Interactional Analysis of Planar and Immersive Workspaces
items.abstract: Remote collaborative platforms increasingly integrate generative AI to support group ideation. These platforms are sociotechnical configurations in which spatial mediation, interaction modality, AI output format, and the mechanisms that make contributions visible to a group co-vary as properties of a deployed system. This paper examines how such configurations shape participants' collaboration and their engagement with AI during creative work. We report a comparative study of two commercially available platforms that instantiate contrasting configurations: a planar shared canvas with text-based AI integration, and an immersive virtual reality workspace with concise AI output embedded in the shared space. Fourteen all-women triads completed a structured ideation task consisting of human-only idea generation, AI-supported idea expansion, and group convergence. We analyzed collaboration patterns, selection of AI-generated ideas, perceived idea quality, workload, presence, and their lexical characteristics. The immersive configuration yielded greater spatial presence and introduced a participation paradox, in which spatial freedom enabled exploration and fragmented group coherence; it was also associated with more balanced role distribution during convergence, at the cost of higher physical demand. In both configurations, AI multiplied the idea pool, and ideas groups authored with AI available were rated above participants' own. AI output format: about 21 words per idea on the planar canvas and 3 in the immersive workspace. Tracked how participants evaluated AI-generated ideas and how often they selected them unaltered as finalists. Neither configuration made AI contributions visible or attributable to the group: participants invoked AI individually and asynchronously in both. We derive design implications for AI output format, group-visible AI invocation, and spatial support for convergence

items.title: Human-AI Collaborative Decision Framework for Distributed Aircraft Power Management in Flight Test Operations
items.abstract: During flight test operations, distributed aircraft power systems are typically managed by human operators through centralized monitoring interfaces. Operators must balance system health, mission objectives, and safety margins under dynamically changing test conditions. However, existing systems are largely reactive and primarily provide fault alerts without predictive insight, which can delay timely intervention and increase operator cognitive workload. This paper proposes a human-AI collaborative decision framework for distributed aircraft power management in flight test environments. The framework integrates predictive health assessment, risk modeling, and strategy evaluation to support operator decision making. A lightweight prognostic mechanism continuously estimates the health risk of individual power cabinets using electrical and thermal indicators. Based on the predicted risk, the system identifies high-risk modules and recommends a small set of feasible power management strategies that balance risk mitigation and mission impact. Human operators remain responsible for final decision selection through a human-centered interface that visualizes system health and strategy options. A simulation-based experimental study using a Wizard-of-Oz platform compares conventional manual management with the proposed Human-AI decision support approach. Results show that the framework improves risk detection efficiency, increases decision accuracy, and reduces unnecessary load shedding. The findings demonstrate the potential of human-AI collaboration to enhance situational awareness and decision performance in safety-critical aircraft power management tasks.

items.title: Human–AI Collaboration and Adaptive Performance: Leadership and Decision Autonomy
items.abstract: The growing integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into organizational work has implications for employee collaboration, technological demands, decision autonomy, and adaptive performance. This study examines the relationships among leadership vision, employee-AI collaboration, techno-overload, AI overreliance, decision autonomy, and adaptive performance. Cross-sectional survey data from 424 respondents were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). The results show that leadership vision is positively associated with employee-AI collaboration and decision autonomy. Employee-AI collaboration is positively associated with AI overreliance, decision autonomy, and adaptive performance, while techno-overload is strongly associated with AI overreliance. Decision autonomy exhibits the strongest direct association with adaptive performance and a significant positive indirect role in the relationship between employee-AI collaboration and adaptive performance. In contrast, the hypothesized negative relationships of techno-overload and AI overreliance with decision autonomy are not supported, nor is the proposed indirect relationship between techno-overload and adaptive performance through decision autonomy. The findings distinguish collaborative AI engagement from reliance-related concerns and highlight the relevance of decision autonomy to employee adaptability. The study contributes to understanding the relationships among organizational leadership, AI-related work experiences, and adaptive performance, offering practical considerations for maintaining employee discretion and responsible AI use in AI-enabled workplaces.

items.title: Integrating iPad-assisted Learning Strategies in High School Science Education: A Critical Narrative Review from a Theoretical Perspective
items.abstract: Tablet computers, and the iPad in particular, have been introduced into secondary schools on a large scale, often through one-to-one programmes justified by claims that portable, touch-based devices will make science learning more engaging, more authentic and more effective. Empirical support for such claims is uneven, and the theoretical reasons why an iPad-assisted activity should or should not improve learning in high school science have rarely been examined together. This critical narrative review synthesises theoretical and empirical literature on iPad-assisted and closely related tablet-assisted learning strategies for students in the upper years of secondary schooling. Literature was identified through structured searches of education-specific and multidisciplinary scholarly indexes, institutional repositories and citation tracking, and was appraised for relevance, design quality and theoretical contribution. The review examines how cognitive load and multimedia learning theory, embodied cognition, inquiry-based and constructivist perspectives, sociocultural and instrumental accounts, generative learning and motivational theory explain the effects of specific strategies, and how integration frameworks such as technological pedagogical content knowledge and the substitution, augmentation, modification and redefinition model have been used, and misused, to guide practice. Strategy-level evidence is strongest for tablets used as experimental tools with multiple linked representations, for well-guided simulations and augmented visualisations, and for student-led or collaborative uses rather than teacher-led display. Meta-analytic averages are generally positive but highly heterogeneous, and they rest heavily on short, small, non-randomised and media-comparison designs, frequently outside the high school age range. Classroom studies repeatedly show that devices are mostly used to replicate existing practice, that teachers' pedagogical knowledge and beliefs condition outcomes, and that distraction, screen-based reading and unequal access remain unresolved concerns. The review proposes an integrative framework in which device affordances influence learning only through specific cognitive, social and motivational mechanisms that are activated by task design, guidance and teacher knowledge. It concludes that the decisive variable is the learning strategy rather than the device, and identifies priorities for theory-testing, longer-term and context-sensitive research.

items.title: Intellectual Tenacity at Work: Generative AI Exposure and the Economic Returns to Occupational Personality Requirements
items.abstract: Technology, including generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), is changing professional work, but its implications for how occupational personality requirements are rewarded in the labor market remain unclear. Using job-incumbent ratings from the U.S. Department of Labor’s Occupational Information Network (O*NET), we identify two personality requirement composites: intellectual tenacity (achievement/effort, persistence, initiative, analytical thinking, innovation, and independence) and social adjustment (emotion regulation, concern for others, social orientation, cooperation, and stress tolerance). We link these measures to more than 15 million workers in the American Community Survey from 2006 to 2024. Intellectual tenacity requirements were positively associated with hourly wages, whereas social adjustment requirements had a weaker, negative association. The wage premium for intellectual tenacity requirements was approximately stable through 2014 and rose thereafter, while the return to social adjustment requirements declined. These divergent trends began before widespread GenAI adoption, but they are concentrated in occupations with greater exposure to GenAI: wage returns for intellectual tenacity requirements increased in occupations highly exposed to GenAI, while returns to social adjustment requirements decreased in those occupations. These findings suggest that broad measures of personality or non-cognitive occupational requirements can obscure opposing shifts in the labor-market value of persistent analytical effort and social adjustment.

items.title: Knowledge Transfer and Talent Development in Traditional Craftsmanship: An HRM Perspective from Atlas Silk
items.abstract: Based on 30 named individual cases documented in public media reports, this paper analyzes the knowledge structure, transmission pathways and talent development challenges associated with Atlas Silk craftsmanship from a human resource management perspective. The B1-B11 framework is used to summarize knowledge content and training arrangements, and the C1-C10 framework is used to identify training, retention and job support issues. The results show that the process and material knowledge can be incorporated into structured training, and the embodied experience of warping, dyeing and weaving still depends on long-term field practice. Families, workshops, cooperatives, colleges and digital communication have complementary functions. To support talent succession, we should combine the phased ability development, compensation guarantee, whole process rotation, dual-mentor training and work design that takes into account the family situation. This paper is a purposively selected literature-based case study, which is not statistically representative.

items.title: Listening and Mirroring: The Effects of Verbal Attunement and Behavioral Mimicry on Social and Empathic Perceptions of Embodied AI Agents in VR
items.abstract: As embodied agents take on increasingly social and relational roles in VR, visual realism and embodiment alone may be insufficient; users must also perceive these agents as emotionally attuned, supportive, and humanlike. Prior work suggests that verbal attunement and nonverbal mimicry can each improve users’ social evaluations of embodied agents. However, behavioral mimicry has largely been studied outside of real-time, conversational AI interactions, leaving limited understanding of how users respond when an agent simultaneously generates contextually responsive dialogue and adapts its nonverbal behavior during an immersive conversation. To address this gap, we developed an embodied AI counselor that combines conversational AI with real-time facial-expression and posture mimicry, while producing either verbally attuned or neutral responses. We evaluated the system in a 2 × 2 within-subjects study with 20 participants, manipulating verbal attunement and behavioral mimicry. Results showed that verbal attunement was the most reliable driver of perceived empathy. Behavioral mimicry showed a marginal relationship with perceived humanness, while greater mimicry exposure showed preliminary, exploratory positive associations with empathy, positivity, and humanness, particularly among female participants. Together, these findings show that multimodal synchrony is not a simple additive strategy for designing empathic conversational agents in VR and underscore the need to consider how verbal and nonverbal behaviors are combined during real-time interaction.

items.title: LLM-Driven Automatic Reward Optimization for Ambient Intelligence Robots with Curriculum Interference Auto-Correction
items.abstract: Service robots in ambient intelligence (AmI) scenarios such as smart factories and home services must rapidly adapt to diverse manipulation tasks, yet traditional reinforcement learning (RL) reward design heavily relies on domain expertise, requiring days to weeks of manual tuning. Existing LLM-assisted reward design methods assume that generated rewards can be directly applied to training environments, overlooking potential incompatibility with built-in training mechanisms such as curriculum learning. To our knowledge, this is the first study to quantify the signal interference phenomenon between LLM-generated rewards and curriculum dynamic weight adjustments---experiments reveal that curriculum modules amplify penalty weights from an initial $-1\times10^{-4}$ to $-0.1$ (a factor of 1000$\times$), overwhelming the positive reward signals---and it proposes an automatic detection and correction mechanism based on feedback ratio anomaly detection. A unified dual-paradigm framework adapting to both ManagerBasedRL and DirectRL paradigms on the IsaacLab platform, along with a humanized interaction paradigm for non-expert users, are also developed. Systematic experiments on five robot tasks of varying difficulty, including ablation studies, 8-sample random search baselines, and multi-seed statistical tests, demonstrate: on Franka Lift the success rate increases from 0\% to 84\%$\pm$2\% and the mean reward from 0.90 to 84.41$\pm$5.50, where simply disabling the curriculum yields a roughly 5$\times$ increase in mean reward (0.90$\rightarrow$4.47)---a necessary prerequisite for LLM reward optimization to take effect---and combining it with the LLM-designed multi-stage reward structure multiplies the improvement by a further 18.9$\times$; under an equal-compute random-search comparison, LLM weight optimization achieves a 47\% improvement over the best random configuration. Mean-reward ratios depend on the reward definition and should be read together with the scale-invariant success rate. The method reduces reward design time from expert-days to hours, validated on the commercial LLM DeepSeek-V4-Pro.

items.title: LLM-ES: A Multi-Agent Hybrid Framework Integrating Large Language Models and Expert Systems for Autonomous Cyber Defense
items.abstract: In recent years, Autonomous Cyber Defense (ACD) methods driven by large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated promising performance in decision interpretability and environmental transferability, yet suffer from low decision efficiency and unstable decision-making. To mitigate these limitations, this work proposes a multi-agent hybrid LLM–expert system framework for ACD. The framework seamlessly integrates the determinism and efficiency of expert systems with the deep reasoning capabilities of LLMs: the expert system makes deterministic decisions based on experiential knowledge, whereas the LLM is responsible for complex decision tasks demanding deep exploration and long-chain reasoning. We further strengthen the LLM via chain-of-thought (CoT) guided prompting, historical memory, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), output alignment and feedback learning. Experimental results demonstrate that incorporating the expert system improves both decision efficiency and defense performance. Evaluated on the CybORG CC4 environment, our approach achieves an average reward of − 98 over ten independent rounds, representing an approximate 25.5% improvement over the best-performing reinforcement learning (RL) baseline. Compared with the standalone LLM method, the average reward increases by roughly 96.2%, while the average per-step runtime is reduced by approximately 14.6%. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to systematically integrate LLMs and expert systems for ACD in the CybORG CC4 environment.

items.title: Measuring the Hermeneutic Circle in Explainable AI: A Human-Free Test Based on Data Horizons, Executable Claims, Part–Whole Agreement, and Machine Readers
items.abstract: Explanations of machine learning models are read by people but rarely evaluated with them, and automatic metrics score attribution vectors rather than what a reader receives. We operationalise the horizon, the hermeneutic circle, and the hermeneutics of suspicion as the Hermeneutic Circle Test (HCT), a human-free screen for explanations of tabular classifiers. HCT checks whether an explanation’s evidence lies inside a calibrated data horizon, whether its sentences survive on-horizon interventions, whether its account of a case agrees with the whole model and at which scale, and whether it helps machine readers learn the model. Over seven explainers, four datasets, and two model families (mean ± standard deviation over eight settings), the best explainer, KernelSHAP, verified 0.65 ± 0.15 of its claims, while random attributions verified 0.22 ± 0.08. On the same explanations, established faithfulness, remove-and-retrain, and disagreement metrics missed impossible evidence and narratives contradicting their own attributions, and sign-blind metrics scored sign-flipped explanations like the originals. Claim tests withstood scaffold attacks that adapt to the horizon and to the test itself; a scaffold that memorises the audited records weakened them and deceived every explainer, but part–whole agreement still flagged it. HCT is a reproducible screen to apply before user studies.

items.abstract: The survey compares two research traditions within the mathematical theory of designing the rules of interaction (mechanisms) for purposeful participants: mechanism design, together with contract theory and implementation theory, and the theory of active systems created by V.N. Burkov and developed into the theory of control in organizations (TCO) by D.A. Novikov's school; the main results of Yu.B. Germeier's school and of the domestic schools adjacent to active systems theory (AST) are covered as well. The problem statements and principal results of 2006-2026 are presented: for mechanism design (MD) - robust and dynamic mechanism design, multidimensional screening, information design, simplicity of mechanisms and credibility of the designer, market design, algorithmic and learning-based design, mechanisms for AI agents, and robust, relational, dynamic and algorithmic contracts; for AST and TCO - a general typology of control, strategy-proof and incentive-compatible planning mechanisms, decomposition of the agents' game, systems with distributed control and coalitional interaction, reflexive games and informational control, control of staff and structure, dynamic active systems, and project management. A correspondence between the classical results is established (the fair play principle and the revelation principle, the serial resource allocation mechanism and the uniform rule, active expertise mechanisms and generalized median schemes, quasi-compensatory incentive schemes and contracts under observable actions), and priorities are delineated by uniform rules; the areas where the two traditions diverge are identified, as are the dimensions of the problem (staff, structure, institutions, awareness, agents' beliefs) covered only by TCO.

items.title: Mediating role of AI-Human Collaboration in the relationship between Artificial Intelligence Adoption and Employee Performance
items.abstract: This study examines the effect of Artificial Intelligence (AI) adoption on employee performance in selected Federal Teaching Hospitals and Federal Medical Centres in Nigeria, with a focus on the mediating role of AI-Human Collaboration. A cross-sectional research design was adopted. The population comprised clinical and non-clinical healthcare workers in selected public healthcare institutions in Nigeria. Using a multistage sampling technique 520 questionnaires were distributed, of which 371 valid responses were analyzed. SmartPLS 4 was employed for data analysis. Findings reveal that AI adoption significantly enhances both AIhuman collaboration and employee performance. AI-human collaboration also has a significant positive effect on employee performance and significantly mediates the relationship between AI adoption and employee performance. The study concludes that AI adoption improves employee performance both directly and indirectly through enhanced collaboration between employees and AI systems. It recommends that healthcare institutions should strengthen AI-human collaboration through continuous training and integration of AI technologies to maximize performance outcomes. These measures are essential for improving workforce efficiency and achieving sustainable performance in Nigeria’s healthcare sector.

items.title: Methodology for Evaluating Artificial Intelligence Chatbots: A Review with Applications to Agricultural Advisory Systems
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence chatbots increasingly advise farmers, yet their adoption should rest on rigorous, standardised evaluation. This review brings together five standardised instruments for assessing chatbots (the System Usability Scale, the Chatbot Usability Scale, the Checklist for Trust between People and Automation, the AI Chatbots Usage Scale, and the User Engagement Scale) and one assessment method, knowledge testing. It also explains Cronbach’s alpha, the reliability criterion most of them rely on. A case study from the literature, in which five large language models answered PhD-level soil science questions, together with deployed systems such as Farmer.Chat and AgroLLM, show how evaluation works in practice and why fluent but unverified advice is risky. Beyond questionnaires, we examine accuracy-based and retrieval-grounded testing. We propose a five-layer protocol that first checks technical accuracy, then usability, trust, engagement, and learning outcomes, to guide the design and validation of chatbots for precision and smallholder farming.

items.title: Mitochondrial capacity limits neuronal energetic feasibility under chronic behavioural stress associated with AI-intensive environments: a neuron–astrocyte genome-scale model of human grey matter
items.abstract: Sustained cognitive engagement, short and mistimed sleep, chronic stress and reduced recovery co-occur in AI-intensive environments, yet how this profile acts on brain energy metabolism is unknown. We built a neuron–astrocyte genome-scale model of human grey matter from Human-GEM v2.1.1, contextualised each cell with human single-nucleus expression, made transport, sodium-pumping and glutathione-recycling costs explicit, and calibrated one parameter to measured cerebral glucose use. Without further fitting the model reproduced the astrocytic share of oxidative metabolism measured by ¹³C spectroscopy (15.7% vs 14%), both the oxidative and the glycolytic regimes of human brain activation, and an independent reconstruction; deletion of genes causing inherited brain-energy disorders compromised its energetic margin far more often than deletion of other genes (odds ratio 79, p = 6 × 10⁻²⁰). Translating the five stressors into constraints, sleep loss and cognitive load each exhausted the margin within the protocol range, at a 25% loss of mitochondrial capacity and a 39% rise in signalling demand, whereas circadian misalignment, chronic stress and reduced recovery acted on arms with reserve. Combined, the stressors exhausted the margin at 0.72 times the moderate profile; across 400 parameter draws demand was met in 99.2% at low and 28.5% at moderate exposure. Substrate oxidation, not substrate supply, set the margin: restoring sleep or reducing load restored it, whereas ketone bodies, lactate or fibre-derived acetate helped only when glucose delivery itself was limiting. Results held across thresholds, releases, solvers and enzyme-capacity limits, and the thresholds are testable with ³¹P and ¹³C spectroscopy.

items.title: Multimodal evaluation of cognitive load during prosthetic device use in activities of daily living
items.abstract: The cognitive burden associated with upper-limb prosthesis use remains a barrier to functional adoption, yet existing evaluations often rely on single-modality measures. This study investigates a multimodal framework for assessing cognitive load during activities of daily living. Twelve participants without limb loss performed standardized activities of daily living using their natural hand and a simulated tendon-driven prosthesis in a within-subject design. This controlled baseline was used to evaluate modality-specific responses to prosthesis-mediated task demands across subjective, behavioral, and neurophysiological measures. Cognitive workload was assessed using task performance metrics, subjective ratings from the NASA Task Load Index (NASA-TLX), eye-tracking measures including gaze behavior and pupillary dynamics, and prefrontal cortical activation measured with functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS). Prosthesis use increased NASA-TLX mental demand by 2.80–3.85 points across tasks (all p < 0.001) and prefrontal oxygenated hemoglobin by 0.96–1.14 μ M across regions during carton transfer and pour (all p < 0.001). Pupillary activity differentiated conditions during block transfer ( p < 0.001) and checker transfer ( p < 0.05), but not carton transfer and pour ( p = 0.47), demonstrating task-dependent responses across modalities. A multimodal framework provides a more comprehensive assessment of cognitive load than any single measure alone, offering valuable insights into how cognitive demand manifests across behavioral, perceptual, and biological domains. This framework establishes a controlled baseline for multimodal cognitive workload assessment and provides a foundation for future investigations in individuals with limb loss.

items.title: NEUROCOGNITIVE AND PSYCHOPHYSIOLOGICAL MECHANISMS OF DRIVER IRRITATION AND OVERLOAD IN RESPONSE TO IN-VEHICLE ALERTS
items.abstract: In-vehicle alerts can support timely responses to hazards, but their sensory and informational demands may also produce annoyance and perceived overload. This scoping review mapped physiological, neurocognitive, and psychophysiological processes investigated or proposed in relation to these responses. Searches in Scopus, APA PsycINFO, and PubMed identified 1,304 records; 955 remained after deduplication, and 16 studies were included in the final synthesis. The synthesis distinguished subjective experiences, physiological indicators, behavioral outcomes, and explanatory mechanisms. Attentional competition, working memory capacity, warning complexity, and presentation timing were relevant to processing demands. Multimodal alerts supported detection and response under some conditions, while also presenting potential costs in startle and intrusiveness. Heart rate variability and electrodermal activity were sensitive to task demands and risk-related arousal, but did not independently identify irritation. Heterogeneity and the absence of formal risk-of-bias assessment limited causal and design conclusions. Future research should combine subjective, physiological, and behavioral measures, separate warning effects from concurrent task and hazard effects, and evaluate repeated exposure and adaptive interfaces in naturalistic driving. Warning assessment should therefore consider tolerability and processing costs alongside response performance.

items.title: Occupational Hazards and Personal Protective Equipment Interventions Relevant to Environmental Health Practitioners in Government Regulatory Services: A Systematic Review of Direct and Indirect Evidence
items.abstract: Environmental Health Practitioners (EHPs) undertake regulatory, inspection and field-based activities that may expose them to multiple occupational hazards. Although personal protective equipment (PPE) is an important occupational risk-control measure, evidence concerning its effectiveness specifically among EHPs remains limited. The study aims to synthesise and evaluate available evidence on occupational hazards and the effectiveness of PPE interventions relevant to EHPs working in government regulatory services. A systematic review was conducted and reported according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. Various Research platforms were searched for peer-reviewed studies published between January 2000 and March 2026. Studies involving EHPs and related regulatory professionals were included, together with relevant evidence from comparable occupational groups where the hazards, exposure pathways or PPE interventions applied to environmental health practice. Due to heterogeneity in study designs, populations, PPE interventions and outcomes, findings were synthesised narratively. Thirty-four unique studies were included. Biological hazards were most frequently reported (82.4%), followed by chemical (47.1%), physical (44.1%), psychosocial (32.4%), organisational/workplace (26.5%), climate/environmental (17.6%) and radiation hazards (2.9%). Respiratory protection was the most frequently reported PPE category (70.6%), followed by gloves (55.9%), protective clothing (41.2%), eye/face protection (35.3%) and protective footwear (20.6%). Overall, appropriately selected PPE reduced occupational exposure; however, effectiveness varied by PPE type and occupational context and was influenced by availability, training, knowledge, adherence, comfort, correct donning and doffing, contamination control, and organisational support. Of the 34 studies, only three directly investigated EHPs, Environmental Health Officers, or Public Health Inspectors. PPE is an important component of occupational protection for EHPs but should be selected according to the specific hazard, task and exposure route and implemented within a broader occupational risk-management approach. The limited direct evidence among environmental health regulatory professionals highlights the need for EHP-specific research to inform PPE guidelines, training and occupational health policies.

items.title: On the Role of Boundary Objects in Agentic Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: Recent advancements in artificial intelligence involve deploying agents that execute tasks and coordinate with one another to produce outputs. These agents, to an extent, mimic human behavior in terms of the need for coordination, in which the output of one agent is used by other agents. The use of agentic AI further underscores the need to verify each agent and their interim outputs to build trustworthiness and ensure reliable final outputs. When agentic AI is used to foster human agency, the output must also be structured to enable desirable, actionable outcomes. In relation to these three areas, the use of artifacts plays an important role, as they can manifest and communicate outputs in a comprehensible manner. These artifacts serve as boundary objects, facilitating knowledge integration and the creation of a common understanding among agents and humans. Boundary object theory can therefore provide a useful lens for understanding agent-to-agent interactions, agent-to-human interactions, and, finally, human-to-human interactions based on the agents’ outputs. In this paper, we present a boundary object perspective that sheds light on facilitating interactions within both technical and sociotechnical systems. We leverage previous research on circular ecosystems to contextualize our discussion, contribute to both agentic AI and boundary object theory, and provide novel insights into the implications of transdisciplinary engineering for the use of agentic AI in complex sociotechnical systems.

items.title: Pedagogical Guidance for the Self-Realisation of High School Students in Extracurricular Activities
items.abstract: Aim. To consider how the features of pedagogical support for extracurricular activities influence the conditions and manifestations of self-realisation of high school students, as well as to establish the relationship between the nature of the environment and key indicators of self-realisation of students.Methodology. The study used a quantitative questionnaire. The survey involved 206 high school students involved in school – based education, and 203 in out-of-school extracurricular providers. Descriptive statistics and comparative analysis were used to identify differences in the perceptions of high school students’ self-actualisation support and the conditions for its implementation in extracurricular activities.Results. It is shown that the specific features of pedagogical support directly influence the conditions and manifestations of self-realisation – key determinants include the subject-subject nature of interaction with adults, support for autonomy and initiative, and developmental feedback. A stable relationship was identified between the characteristics of the organisational environment and key indicators of self-realisation. In out-of-school extracurricular providers, where voluntary participation and a horizontal interaction structure prevail, high school students demonstrate a significantly higher level of agency, self-organisation, critical thinking, and activity satisfaction, while the impact on self-awareness and career self-determination is deeper and more deliberate. In the school environment, oriented toward formal control and academic requirements, self-realisation more often retains a situational character, and the space for equitable dialogue and support of personal initiatives remains limited. The obtained data confirm that it is precisely the quality of pedagogical support and the type of educational environment that determine the depth and sustainability of self-realisation processes among high school students in extracurricular activities.Scientific novelty and research implications. The scientific novelty of this study lies in several key aspects. Firstly, it empirically establishes that the nature of pedagogical guidance (namely subject-to-subject interaction, autonomy support, and developmental feedback), rather than the mere formal availability of opportunities, serves as a crucial condition for the depth and sustainability of high school students’ self-realisation. Secondly, a robust correlation was identified between the type of organisational environment and key self-realisation metrics: voluntary and horizontal structures in extracurricular organisations statistically correlate with significantly higher levels of agency, self-awareness, and career self-determination compared to formalised school environments. Thirdly, the study proposes an operationalisation of self-realisation in extracurricular activities through a system of measurable indicators linking the quality of pedagogical interaction with students' personal outcomes. The theoretical significance consists in clarifying of the “self-realisation” concept through the prism of intrinsic motivation, as well as in demonstrating the differentiated potential of two key institutions – schools and out-of-school extracurricular providers – in creating conditions for genuine rather than situational self-realisation. The practical significance of the results lies in the possibility of using them to improve the practices of pedagogical support in schools: the transition from directive control to partner mentoring, the development of teachers’ competencies in the field of facilitation and tutoring, as well as the integration of school and out-of-school extracurricular providers resources.Conclusions. 1. A comparison of models revealed that the effectiveness of pedagogical support depends less on the type of institution and more on the nature of interaction, specifically through supporting student autonomy and initiative within a subject-subject communication framework. 2. High school students’ self-realization (manifested in agency, self-organisation, and critical thinking) is significantly associated with voluntary participation and the provision of developmental feedback. 3. The impact of extracurricular activities on self-awareness and career self-determination is strengthened by integrating reflective practices and providing opportunities for students to implement personal initiatives. 4. Satisfaction with activities correlates with the quality of pedagogical interaction, with key facilitating factors being intrinsic motivation, equitable dialogue, and a trusting environment. 5. Enhancing school-based practices is best achieved by integrating effective approaches, including developing teachers’ tutoring competencies, increasing format flexibility, and fostering network collaboration with out-of-school extracurricular providers.

items.title: People analytics in employee performance management: A bibliometric mapping and structured content review
items.abstract: People analytics is increasingly being used to measure, track and improve performance. The research in this area, however, is highly fragmented across disciplines and the results are mixed. This paper maps the thematic and intellectual structure of the field and synthesizes the evidence on the impact of people analytics on performance management. It combines a bibliometric analysis of the Scopus indexed literature with a structured content review of the full text studies. There has been a significant increase in the volume of publications over recent years with HR analytics, AI and HRM forming the core of the keyword network. Bibliographic coupling reveals four tentative theoretical streams emerging over time: from incentive economics to organizational capability, then to a more behavioral focus on fairness and finally to the more recent generative AI work which largely reuses the existing frameworks. The content review suggests that people analytics can improve measurement, prediction and feedback, but the extent of this is contingent upon the quality of the data, the design of the metrics, the presence of complementary management practices, the level of managerial support and employee trust. A number of the studies point to trade-offs between the quality and quantity of output and between the technical accuracy of the analytics and employee acceptance. items.title: Perspective Chapter: Designing for Life Beyond Earth – From Ergonomic Gloves to Living Regolith: A Human-Centred Framework for Mars: Ergonomics, Materials and Well-Being Across Three Original Design Case Studies for Mars Habitability
items.abstract: Discussions of Mars exploration have long been dominated by propulsion, trajectory, and payload. Yet the most complex system in any deep-space mission is neither the rocket nor the habitat structure: it is the human being inside it. This chapter argues that design – understood in its fullest sense, from ergonomics and environmental psychology to participatory and systems-level human-centred approaches – must be repositioned as a first-order engineering and policy concern, not an afterthought applied once structural decisions have been made. This chapter examines how design thinking, human factors, and habitability science must evolve to support sustained human presence on Mars. This work explains how the role of designers is fundamental within an interdisciplinary team in which different skills intersect and complement one another. This is illustrated through three original design research projects, reviewed and presented at international conferences: a bio-based printable construction material, a 4D self-assembling shelter, and a haptic wearable device for augmented perception, thereby arguing that human-centred design, ergonomics, and astronaut well-being must be repositioned as first-order constraints in Mars mission architecture.

items.title: Practices of Human-AI Collaboration in Enterprise Generative AI Adoption and Their Implications for Organisational Digital Innovation
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence is beginning to be used in enterprise workflows as a flexible generator of text, code, images, summaries, and conversations. However, the organisation's value is not derived from technology alone. This conceptual paper explores how enterprises can organise human-AI collaboration during the adoption process and what such practices may achieve for digital innovation. Differentiate among support, sequential co-creation, iterative co-creation and supervised delegation; link these models to workflow redesign, knowledge sharing, service improvement and innovation capabilities. Based on the above discussion, the conditions for converting model outputs into responsible organisational behaviour are task decomposition, verification, role clarity, learning routines and governance. It will also solve hallucination, bias, confidentiality, deskilling, over-reliance and unequal participation. No original data, field research, experiments or performance tests were conducted. Therefore, this paper provides mechanisms and practice-oriented suggestions instead of causal results. It believes that generative AI should be treated as a fallible organisational participant in sociotechnical arrangements, and people are responsible for the goals, contextual judgement, verification and consequential decisions.

items.title: PRELIMINARY ERGONOMIC ANALYSIS OF HEALTHCARE PROFESSIONALS’ WORKING CONDITIONS IN A BRAZILIAN UNIVERSITY HOSPITAL EMERGENCY UNIT
items.abstract: This study analyzed the working conditions of healthcare professionals in the emergency and urgency unit of a Brazilian University Hospital using a preliminary ergonomic analysis. The method comprised two tools: the Ergonomic Checklist and the Self-Assessment Tool Ergonomics/Human Factors questionnaire. These instruments facilitated the assessment of physical, cognitive, and organizational demands within the occupational environment. The findings highlighted critical ergonomic issues, such as inadequate furniture, excessive noise, and poor lighting conditions. A high level of physical strain was noted due to the intense work pace and constant movement required, while cognitive demands were marked by time pressure, mental overload, and emotional stress. Organizational deficiencies, particularly those related to communication, were also identified as factors compromising task execution and workplace safety. The study underscores the need for ergonomic interventions, including workload adjustments, planned breaks, environmental adaptations, psychological support programs, and improved internal communication strategies. These measures aim to reduce physical and cognitive strain, promote healthier and safer working conditions, and improve the quality of patient care. Moreover, the proposed method can be systematically applied to other hospital units to determine whether the identified demands are specific to the studied unit or indicative of broader systemic challenges within the hospital environment.

items.title: Problem jakości wiedzy generowanej przez AI w decyzjach menedżerskich
items.abstract: Artykuł analizuje jakość wiedzy generowanej przez sztuczną inteligencję w decyzjach menedżerskich. Punktem wyjścia jest teza, że użyteczność decyzyjna odpowiedzi tworzonych przez GenAI nie wynika z ich stylistycznej płynności, lecz z nadzoru epistemicznego, który łączy wynik działania modelu ze źródłami, kryteriami, kontekstem, aktualnością oraz odpowiedzialnością. Część empiryczna ma charakter porównawczego studium wielu przypadków i opiera się na publicznie udokumentowanych wdrożeniach: IBM AskHR w obszarze HR, BMW Group Offer Analyst w zakupach, AI @ Morgan Stanley Assistant i Debrief w doradztwie finansowym, ConsumerIQ w The Estée Lauder Companies oraz Lilli w McKinsey. Analizę uzupełnia warstwa kontrolna zaczerpnięta z badań eksperymentalnych nad GenAI w pracy wiedzochłonnej, zwłaszcza eksperymentu z konsultantami Boston Consulting Group dotyczącego tak zwanej poszarpanej granicy technologicznej. W artykule rozwinięto ramę JWG-AI, która obejmuje sześć wymiarów jakości wiedzy: trafność merytoryczną, możliwość prześledzenia dowodów, kompletność względem kryteriów, adekwatność kontekstową, aktualność czasową i bezpieczeństwo normatywne. Wyniki wskazują, że wysoka jakość wdrożeń GenAI zależy mniej od samej mocy modelu, a bardziej od kuratorowanych korpusów, dyscypliny wyszukiwania, jawnych kryteriów, rutyn ewaluacyjnych, ścieżek eskalacji i odpowiedniego nadzoru człowieka.

items.title: PSYCHOPHYSIOLOGICAL DEVELOPMENT CHARACTERISTICS OF PRIMARY SCHOOL STUDENTS AND THE ROLE OF PLAY ACTIVITIES IN ENHANCING THEIR COGNITIVE ENGAGEMENT
items.abstract: The psychophysiological development of primary school children is fundamental for their academic success, yet the systematic integration of play to enhance cognitive engagement, especially its specific mechanisms, remains understudied. The aim of this study is to investigate primary school children's psychophysiological development and play's role in enhancing cognitive engagement. This article explores the intricate link between psychophysiological maturation—including brain development, motor skills, sensory processing, and emotional regulation—and cognitive engagement. It examines how these developmental trajectories influence learning and how play-based strategies can bridge developmental gaps. The text highlights that rapid brain development, particularly in the prefrontal cortex, enhances executive functions, inhibitory control, working memory, and cognitive flexibility. It emphasizes that myelination improves neural transmission, while refined motor and sensory skills, alongside evolving emotional regulation, are crucial for sustained attention and active participation. Understanding these developmental aspects is vital for educators to tailor learning experiences that optimize children's potential for cognitive engagement and academic success through effective pedagogical approaches.

items.title: Reflective, Experiential and Coaching-Based Workplace Learning in Service Organisations A Systematic Literature Review
items.abstract: Service organisations depend on frontline employees whose competence is built largely at work, yet evidence on structured workplace learning remains fragmented. This systematic literature review synthesises empirical evidence on reflective, experiential and coaching-based learning among in-service workers and identifies the organisational conditions that shape it. Following PRISMA 2020, 97 open-access journal articles published between 2021 and 2026 were retrieved from Scopus and screened against set eligibility criteria. Twenty-nine studies were included, appraised with the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool and synthesised thematically. The evidence was dominated by healthcare and human services in high-income countries, qualitative designs and self-reported outcomes. Five themes emerged, (1) reflection works best when built into daily work; (2) real work experience builds skills when it matches the job; (3) coaching and feedback depend on prepared coaches and trust; (4) peers and groups spread new practice across teams; and (5) workplace conditions, such as supervisor support, psychological safety, hierarchy and workload, decide whether learning is used. The review proposes a structured workplace learning cycle linking these elements. Workplace learning becomes sustainable when it is built into daily work and supported by supervisors. Stronger behavioural evidence is needed from Southeast Asian and frontline service sectors such as private security.

items.title: Relación de la ergonomía con la calidad de vida del docente universitario
items.abstract: Introduction: University professors, immersed in demanding and highly technologized work environments, face conditions that compromise their physical, cognitive, emotional, and social well-being. In this context, ergonomics emerges as a key discipline to mitigate disergonomic risks and foster healthy work environments. Objective: Characterize the relationship between ergonomic factors (physical, cognitive, organizational, and environmental) and the quality of life of university professors, based on the most recent scientific evidence. Methods: An integrative review of scientific literature published between 2019 and 2024 was conducted in the databases Scopus, Web of Science, PubMed, SciELO, and Redalyc. Search strategies combined Boolean operators (“ergonom*” AND “university professor” AND “quality of life”) with equivalent MeSH and DeCS terms. Eligible documents included peer-reviewed articles, empirical studies, systematic reviews, and meta-analyses. Inclusion criteria considered thematic relevance, methodological rigor, and full-text availability. A total of 52 studies met the inclusion criteria. Results: Ergonomic factors are closely associated with the overall well-being of university faculty. Ergonomic interventions improve musculoskeletal health, reduce cognitive fatigue, promote job satisfaction, and optimize the environmental conditions of academic work. Conclusions: Ergonomics, when addressed holistically and at the institutional level, represents a key strategy for enhancing the quality of life of university professors. Its systematic implementation fosters professional performance and helps prevent occupational diseases.

items.title: Revisiting warranting theory in AI-mediated communication: An evaluation of writer and source effects in online reviews.
items.abstract: This article examines how attributing the actual writer of an online message to artificial intelligence (AI) , rather than a human, shapes impression formation . By drawing on and extending warranting theory, this article examines how source role labels (self vs. third party) and content writer labels (AI vs. human) interact to affect impression formation and message effects in the context of hotel reviews. Two preregistered experiments (Study 1: N = 461; Study 2: N = 444) found that, for the same positive hotel review, third-party reviewers were perceived more favorably than self-reviewers (i.e., hotel managers), leading to more positive evaluations of the hotel. Reviews attributed to AI writers negatively impacted impressions of the reviewer and diminished the review’s impact, with third-party reviewers more negatively affected by AI writer labels than self-reviewers. AI labels of user-generated content, therefore, attenuate the effects of source role and move people out of their default impression formation state. We demonstrate theoretical advancements for warranting theory and AI-mediated communication.

items.title: Scaffolded large language model feedback builds durable translation competence whereas unrestricted use fosters dependency
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are rapidly entering translator education, yet it remains unclear whether they build students' own translation competence or merely improve the products students submit. We combined a validation study on public benchmark data with a 16-week quasi-experiment to test a scaffolded human--LLM pedagogy, the Draft--Diagnose--Revise--Reflect (D2R) cycle, for English--Chinese translation. In Study 1, a rubric-guided error-annotation prompt increased the agreement between LLM feedback and expert Multidimensional Quality Metrics judgements on 2,500 WMT segments for all four models tested; with this prompt GPT-4o reached a segment-level Kendall's $\tau$ of 0.30, on a par with the strongest neural metric, and the highest error-detection accuracy. In Study 2, 179 English majors received conventional instruction, unrestricted LLM access or the guardrailed D2R cycle. Unrestricted access maximised LLM-assisted performance but yielded no advantage in unassisted translation over conventional instruction at a delayed test 12 weeks after the course (Hedges' $g$ = $-$0.08) and produced the largest AI-dependency gap. Scaffolded use produced durable gains in unassisted translation ($g$ = 0.70), a 13\% reduction in error rate and higher metacognitive regulation. Process logs indicated that the benefit was transmitted mainly through lower verbatim adoption of LLM output. Pedagogical design, not LLM access per se, determines whether LLMs support or supplant translation learning.

items.title: Short-term cognitive impairments during night work: a meta-analysis and systematic review
items.abstract: Cognitive performance is used as a proxy for work performance and safety. This meta -analysis and systematic review compared cognitive performance during night shifts (23:00–07:00) with daytime performance (07:00–23:00) across experimental field and laboratory studies, excluding shifts exceeding 24 h. Meta-regressions examined night shift, study context, and cognitive test characteristics as sources of heterogeneity. Fifty-five studies were included, yielding 758 night work and 964 daytime datapoints from 1,919 participants, combined into 6135 effect sizes. Cognitive performance was impaired during night shifts relative to daytime hours (Hedges g = −0.36, 95% CI [−0.49, −0.23], p < 0.001), although indications of publication bias suggest this pooled estimate is somewhat inflated. Impairments increased with time into the shift, from 0:01–08:59 h (g = −0.33, 95% CI [−0.63, −0.02], p = 0.041) to > 9 h (g = −0.61, 95% CI [−0.96, −0.25], p = 0.004). Impairments were more pronounced on simple tests (g = −0.50, 95% CI [−0.70, −0.31], p < 0.001), as complex tests weakened the night-daytime difference (g = 0.29, 95% CI [0.07, 0.50], p < 0.001). This contrast was driven by the Psychomotor Vigilance Test (PVT); excluding PVT data removed the difference and attenuated the pooled effect to g = −0.24. No significant moderating effects emerged for time point during the shift, shift sequence, test outcome, or study context (field vs. laboratory). Extended night shifts thus appear detrimental to safety, with heightened sensitivity concentrated in psychomotor vigilance type tasks. Both contexts appear valid for examining these effects. Remaining heterogeneity warrants further investigation of environmental and individual factors.

items.title: Socratic AI: A bitter but effective pill for moral enhancement
items.abstract: Socratic AI uses questioning to induce reflection on one’s own moral stance. Normative literature often favors Socratic over advisory AI for ethical enhancement because it is thought to respect moral autonomy by avoiding direct steering of moral judgments, yet its behavioral impact remains underexplored. We report a behavioral online experiment in which participants faced a moral trade-off between efficiency and equality in a politically polarized context where partisan identity could illegitimately bias decisions. Participants made distributive choices with real monetary consequences either without AI support or after live interaction with AI-based chatbots prompt-engineered to follow either a Socratic questioning style or an advisory, recommendation-giving style. Because it is unclear how a non-directive AI would influence moral choices relative to a No-AI baseline, we treated this comparison as an open, exploratory empirical question. Compared with the No-AI baseline, Socratic AI reduced political ingroup favoritism without systematically shifting participants’ average choices along the efficiency-equality trade-off. The estimated reduction of political ingroup favoritism under Advisory AI was descriptively smaller and statistically inconclusive. Moreover, participants’ average choices after interacting with the efficiency-focused and equality-focused variants of advisory AI diverged significantly from each other in the direction of the respective endorsed principles. Despite these encouraging behavioral results regarding Socratic AI, participants evaluated advisory AI more favorably than Socratic AI and expressed a stronger preference for it. Our findings suggest that Socratic AI is a promising route to ethical enhancement through moral debiasing, provided user-acceptance challenges can be addressed.

items.title: Spatial Visual Guides: Supporting Spatial Thinking Through Multimodal Hand Interaction in VR
items.abstract: Assembling objects in Virtual Reality using hand actions is cognitively demanding because users must identify relationships among components. We present Spatial Visual Guides (SVG), a novel user interface that provides context-sensitive visual guides designed to scaffold users’ spatial reasoning during 3D assembly tasks. Users invoke SVG automatically through naturalistic hand actions (Hand-SVG) or deliberately through a multimodal combination of voice and hand input (VoiceHand-SVG). In a user study, 24 participants performed a 3D assembly task at two levels of complexity (easy and hard) using SVG. We found a difference in usage between the multimodal VoiceHand-SVG interface and Hand-SVG: VoiceHand-SVG produced fewer guide activations while remaining visible for similar durations. Moreover, participants’ articulated strategies and behavioural logs helped us understand how participants used SVGs during assembly, and showed that participants used SVGs for orientation anchoring, relational comparison, and placement planning. SVGs also improved task performance compared to no visual feedback. Our results demonstrate the advantages of designing visual guides around specific spatial reasoning behaviours, and reveal trade-offs between unimodal and multimodal interaction strategies.

items.title: Students’ engagement and perceived effectiveness of Wordwall activities for ESL sentence construction
items.abstract: This study investigated students' behavioural, emotional and cognitive engagement, and their perceived effectiveness of Wordwall, following the use of Wordwall activities in English sentence construction lessons in one secondary school in Malaysia. While digital and game-based learning are gaining traction in the language classroom, constructing sentences can be a challenge for language learners and may need to be practised multiple times with feedback and active engagement. A quantitative descriptive survey design was employed with 55 Form 1 and Form 2 students from four classes in one secondary school in Malaysia. The participants engaged in three Wordwall-based sentence construction sessions followed by a post-intervention questionnaire that measured behavioural, emotional and cognitive engagement and the perceived effectiveness of Wordwall. The data were analysed using frequencies, means, standard deviations and Cronbach's alpha to assess the internal consistency of the questionnaire scales. The results showed that self-reported engagement scores were moderately positive across all three dimensions, with emotional engagement recording the highest mean score (M = 3.45, SD = 0.85), followed by cognitive engagement (M = 3.42, SD = 0.82) and behavioural engagement (M = 3.34, SD = 0.84); however, differences among the three dimensions were small. Students also reported moderately positive perceptions of the effectiveness of Wordwall for learning sentence construction (M = 3.28, SD = 1.09). These findings suggest that Wordwall may serve as a supplementary tool in interactive and participatory sentence construction lessons. However, the study did not measure learning gains, no control group was used, and the small convenience sample limits generalisation; the results therefore reflect students' self-reported perceptions only. Future research should incorporate objective measures of learning and stronger comparative designs in ESL classrooms. Kajian ini meneliti penglibatan tingkah laku, emosi dan kognitif pelajar serta persepsi mereka terhadap keberkesanan Wordwall susulan penggunaan aktiviti Wordwall dalam pengajaran pembinaan ayat bahasa Inggeris di sebuah sekolah menengah di Malaysia. Walaupun pembelajaran digital dan pembelajaran berasaskan permainan semakin mendapat tempat dalam bilik darjah bahasa, pembinaan ayat boleh menjadi cabaran kepada pelajar dan mungkin memerlukan latihan berulang dengan maklum balas serta penglibatan aktif. Reka bentuk tinjauan deskriptif kuantitatif digunakan melibatkan 55 orang pelajar Tingkatan 1 dan Tingkatan 2 daripada empat kelas di sebuah sekolah menengah di Malaysia. Peserta kajian mengambil bahagian dalam tiga sesi pembinaan ayat berasaskan Wordwall yang diikuti dengan soal selidik pascaintervensi untuk mengukur penglibatan tingkah laku, emosi dan kognitif serta persepsi terhadap keberkesanan Wordwall. Data dianalisis menggunakan kekerapan, min, sisihan piawai dan alfa Cronbach bagi menilai ketekalan dalaman skala soal selidik tersebut. Dapatan kajian menunjukkan bahawa skor penglibatan yang dilaporkan sendiri oleh pelajar berada pada tahap sederhana positif merentasi ketiga-tiga dimensi, dengan penglibatan emosi mencatatkan skor min tertinggi (M = 3.45, SD = 0.85), diikuti oleh penglibatan kognitif (M = 3.42, SD = 0.82) dan penglibatan tingkah laku (M = 3.34, SD = 0.84). Walau bagaimanapun, perbezaan antara ketiga-tiga dimensi tersebut adalah kecil. Pelajar juga melaporkan persepsi yang sederhana positif terhadap keberkesanan Wordwall dalam pembelajaran pembinaan ayat (M = 3.28, SD = 1.09). Dapatan ini menunjukkan bahawa Wordwall berpotensi digunakan sebagai alat sokongan dalam pengajaran pembinaan ayat secara interaktif dan melibatkan penyertaan aktif pelajar. Namun demikian, kajian ini tidak mengukur peningkatan hasil pembelajaran, tiada kumpulan kawalan digunakan, dan saiz sampel mudah yang kecil membataskan kebolehumuman dapatan. Oleh itu, dapatan kajian ini hanya mencerminkan persepsi yang dilaporkan sendiri oleh pelajar. Kajian pada masa hadapan wajar menggunakan pengukuran hasil pembelajaran secara objektif serta reka bentuk kajian perbandingan yang lebih kukuh dalam bilik darjah bahasa Inggeris sebagai bahasa kedua (ESL).

items.title: Supporting Researcher Control in AI-Assisted Social Media Analysis: A Mixed-Methods Study of AI4OSN
items.abstract: High-quality annotated datasets are critical for advancing computational social science (CSS) research, yet collecting, curating, and analyzing large-scale data from dynamic sources such as online social networks (OSNs) remains a persistent bottleneck. Researchers must also translate substantive questions into queries, relevance criteria, and defensible interpretations. Large language models (LLMs) can assist, but they can also obscure the judgments, potentially reducing researcher oversight and critical evaluation. We present AI4OSN, a mixed-initiative platform that keeps researchers in control of data collection, relevance labeling, and sensemaking while making AI assistance available as an inspectable advisory resource. In a systematic user study (N=18) using X/Twitter data, participants reported above-benchmark perceived usability (mean SUS score of 79.7), increased confidence in LLM-assisted annotation and analysis tasks, and low cognitive workload during AI-supported sensemaking. Notably, novice participants showed descriptively greater alignment and higher reported agreement with AI output than experienced participants, underscoring the need to support differentiated verification practices across expertise levels. Overall, this work contributes both a human-centered system for social data analysis and empirical insights into how AI-assisted interfaces shape researcher behavior, trust, and decision-making. Our findings highlight design opportunities and tensions in building accessible, transparent, and agentic AI systems for social media and web research.

items.title: Task-level assessment of robotic solutions in warehouses: a human-centric framework
items.abstract: Technological advancements are transforming warehouse operations, as robotic solutions are increasingly deployed to enhance efficiency and productivity. Although these technologies reduce physical strain and automate repetitive tasks, their broader effects on human factors (HFs), including perceptual, mental, physical, and psychosocial dimensions, remain insufficiently understood. Moreover, explicit links between specific robotic capabilities and task-level effects on workers remain limited. To address this gap, this study develops a human-centric, task-level framework for evaluating how different robotic solutions influence HFs in warehouse operations. Using an exploratory, qualitative, multi-method approach, the study triangulates insights from literature, practitioner discussions, robotics solution providers, and end users to classify robotic solutions according to interaction level, task-execution roles, and adaptability. Application of the framework to the key warehouse task of order picking shows that robotic solutions reduce physical workload while introducing mixed mental and perceptual demands related to supervision and monitoring, and psychosocial challenges associated with shared-space interaction and job engagement. These findings highlight the importance of early human-centric evaluation during technology selection and implementation, enabling organisations to anticipate potential benefits and challenges prior to deployment. The framework supports human-centric decision-making in warehouse robotics and provides a basis for future empirical research on task-level human–robot interaction (HRI).

items.title: Teachers’ Perceptions about Digitalization of Teaching and its Influence on Students’ Engagement at GS Kagugu, Rwanda
items.abstract: The digitalization of teaching has become a global educational priority aimed at enhancing student engagement and promoting learner-centered instruction.In Rwanda, national initiatives such as the ICT in Education Policy and Smart Classroom Project seek to integrate digital technologies into classroom practices.However, limited evidence exists regarding teachers' perceptions of digitalization and its influence on student engagement at the school level.This qualitative case study explored secondary school teachers' perceptions of the digitalization of teaching and its influence on students' behavioral, emotional, and cognitive engagement at GS Kagugu in Gasabo District, Rwanda.Guided by Constructivist Learning Theory and the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), the study employed an interpretivist paradigm using semi-structured interviews and document analysis.Five purposively selected teachers from different subject areas participated in the study.Thematic analysis revealed that teachers conceptualize digitalization either as the substitution of traditional instructional tools or as a pedagogical transformation that promotes learner-centered and interactive learning.The findings indicated that digital teaching practices positively influence student motivation, participation, attention, and conceptual understanding when effectively integrated.However, challenges including unstable internet connectivity, power interruptions, limited digital competencies, and inadequate professional development constrain meaningful technology integration.The study recommends continuous school-based professional development, peer-led mentoring initiatives, equitable access to digital resources, and the provision of localized offline-capable digital learning materials.Educational digitalization should therefore prioritize teacher capacity building alongside technological investments to maximize student engagement and learning outcomes.
