items.title: Teaching Fast, High-Precision Skills in Mixed Reality: A Terminal Feedback System for Iaido
items.abstract: Mixed Reality (MR) movement applications for consumers are mostly games and exergames, while research systems that target skill acquisition typically rely on external motion capture or enterprise headsets. Fast, ballistic motions such as a sword strike are completed too quickly to correct mid-movement, so motor-learning theory favors terminal over concurrent feedback. We present a first-person MR system for the unmodified Meta Quest 3 that captures a full strike, compares it against a demonstrator’s reference, and delivers terminal feedback: Knowledge of Performance (KP), a line-based visualization of path and blade-orientation error, and Knowledge of Result (KR), a summary verdict. Iaido, a Japanese sword-drawing art whose strikes demand both a correct path and an aligned cutting edge, serves as the precision testbed. In a within-subjects crossover study (n = 16), novices practiced with and without this feedback, each block followed by an immediate feedback-free post-test, and reported workload (NASA-TLX) and intrinsic motivation (IMI). During guided practice, blade-angle error was lower than during unguided practice (Δ = −6.7°, p = 0.010, dz = −0.74). At the post-test it was lower but not significant (dz = −0.56); delayed retention was not tested. Path deviation was lower but not significant, with the residual error mainly in depth along the line of sight. Workload was higher but not significantly so, and intrinsic motivation stayed high. These results point to an accuracy–workload trade-off for reference-based terminal feedback in fast-motion MR training, established against unassisted practice, which simulates self-training.

items.title: The Effect of gamification on students’ motivation in secondary schools in Enugu north LGA, Enugu State, Nigeria
items.abstract: Introduction: Student motivation influences learners’ willingness to initiate, sustain and complete academic tasks. Gamification introduces selected game-design elements into instruction and may influence both intrinsic and extrinsic motivation. Purpose: This study examined the effect of gamification on the intrinsic and extrinsic motivation of Senior Secondary School One (SS1) students in Enugu North Local Government Area, Enugu State, Nigeria. Methodology: A quasi-experimental, non-equivalent control-group design was used with 160 SS1 students from four public secondary schools. Eighty students were assigned to the experimental group and 80 to the control group. The experimental group received four weeks of instruction incorporating points, badges, leaderboards, challenges and feedback, while the control group received conventional instruction. Data were collected with the Students’ Motivation Questionnaire and analysed using means, standard deviations and independent-samples t-tests. Results: The experimental group recorded higher reported mean scores than the control group for intrinsic motivation (3.52 versus 2.81), t(158) = 6.90, p < .001, and extrinsic motivation (3.50 versus 2.87), t(158) = 6.22, p < .001. Conclusion: The group comparisons indicate that students exposed to gamified instruction reported higher intrinsic- and extrinsic-motivation scores than students receiving conventional instruction. Recommendation: Teachers should align game elements with learning objectives and combine recognition and rewards with meaningful challenges, learner choice and informative feedback.

items.title: The Intrinsic Drivers of Employee Retention: Reassessment of Organizational Justice Theory in a Resource Constrained Context
items.abstract: This study challenges the assumption that distributive justice remains a dominant driver of employee retention in resource‑constrained contexts. Drawing on Organizational Justice Theory, Self‑Determination Theory, and Two‑Factor Theory, the research examines how job satisfaction, work–life balance, distributive justice, and perceived job quality influence employees’ intention to stay within a private sector healthcare environment. The study investigates whether distributive fairness still remains a dominant driver of retention in an economically constrained environment. Using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS‑SEM) on survey data from 177 employees across multiple settings, results indicate that job satisfaction and work–life balance significantly predict intention to stay, whereas distributive justice and perceived job quality do not. The findings suggest that intrinsic motivational factors tend to supersede distributive fairness considerations in a limited resourced context, thereby offering boundary conditions for justice‑based retention frameworks. Its implications for contextualized HRM theory and retention strategy are further discussed.

items.title: The role of artificial intelligence in green human resource management and organizational sustainability: a systematic literature review and bibliometric analysis
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly presented as the technology that will allow green human resource management (GHRM) to deliver organizational sustainability, yet the evidence behind this claim is recent, scattered and largely unexamined. This study combines a PRISMA-guided systematic literature review with a VOSviewer-based bibliometric analysis to establish what is known, how it is known and what remains untested. A Scopus search (12 November 2026) returned 297 records; after document-type filtering and title–abstract–keyword screening, 97 journal articles and reviews formed the mapping corpus, and two further eligible articles were added to the critical synthesis (n = 99). Keyword co-occurrence, overlay, co-citation, bibliographic coupling and country co-authorship maps were produced, and every study was coded for the structural role assigned to AI, theory, method, context and outcome. The field is young (77.3% of the corpus is published from 2025–2026), geographically limited (mostly emerging Asian countries), and methodologically homogeneous, with 44 of 62 quantitative studies using cross-sectional structural equation modelling of self-reported data. Five roles for AI are discussed (enabler, amplifier, mediator, complementary resource and embedded practice), but they are often mixed up, or not well explained theoretically. The conceptual foundations are the resource-based view and the GHRM foundations and the critical literature on algorithmic management is not present in the co-citation structure. These are flanked by reports in other studies of non-significant and negative effects, as well as no environmental footprint for AI itself, meaning the current optimism is premature. The paper introduces a typology of AI roles and a socio-technical capability-conversion framework that consists of six propositions, and a research agenda.

items.title: Threat Landscape of Vibe Coding and the Road to Secure Autonomy
items.abstract: Vibe coding is reshaping software development, enabling faster implementation and allowing individuals with limited programming experience to describe requirements in natural language while AI agents write, test, and deploy the code. As these agents evolve into autonomous systems that execute commands, manage dependencies, access cloud resources, and interact with other agents, their security risks extend beyond incorrect code to actions with direct consequences for software systems. Although research on these risks is expanding, it remains fragmented across areas including prompt injection, insecure code generation, supply-chain attacks, and human factors, with limited consensus on terminology, threat assumptions, and evaluation. This paper consolidates emerging research through the lens of the vibe coding workflow. We establish a reference architecture, characterise six levels of agent autonomy, and develop a threat model centred on five trust boundaries spanning developers, AI models, tools, cloud infrastructure, and the wider software ecosystem. Building on this foundation, we propose a taxonomy of twenty-one threats across nine classes. For each threat, we review the available evidence, assess proposed defences, and identify limitations. Our analysis highlights that risks increase with agents' operational authority, while most defences rely on model judgement and address isolated threats. Finally, we identify eleven research challenges, including enforceable limits on agent authority and shared benchmarks and methodologies for assessing vibe coding security.

items.title: Towards New Materialist Informatics as a Critical Technical Practice
items.abstract: This chapter closes the book with an argument for New Materialist Informatics as a transdisciplinary critical technical practice. It discusses the diagrammatics of machine learning as a framework of knowledge production as well as of power in machine learning systems. Positioning machine learning systems as complex assemblages, the chapter argues that the analysis and design of such systems require transdisciplinary critical approaches. A synthetic field of New Materialist Informatics is introduced as one such transdisciplinary practice, which brings together research and epistemology of new materialisms together with sociotechnical design practices. A method of transposition is proposed as a way to activate feminist new materialist conceptual foundations for technical practice.

items.title: Towards Trustworthy Multi-Agent Cybersecurity Architectures for Financial Critical Infrastructures
items.abstract: Financial critical infrastructures face mounting cyber threats across heterogeneous, fragmented digital ecosystems. Existing Security Operations Centre architectures, spanning SIEM platforms, XDR systems, and threat intelligence feeds, lack the contextual reasoning, governance alignment, and explainability that highly regulated environments require. We propose a trustworthy multi-agent cybersecurity architecture that integrates LLM-enhanced contextual orchestration grounded in shared semantic security knowledge, human-in-the-loop governance, compliance-aware runtime control, and collaborative threat intelligence. Rather than treating cyber resilience as a purely technical detection problem, our framework conceptualises it as a socio-technical orchestration challenge explicitly designed to support compliance with DORA, NIS2, GDPR, PSD2, and the EU AI Act. We describe a six-layer architecture, analyse its governance and resilience implications, and identify open research challenges. The central argument is that AI agents should augment cybersecurity professionals, not replace them, preserving human authority over high-stakes decisions while reducing alert fatigue and enabling privacy-preserving collaborative defence across institutions.

items.title: Trust Contagion and Transfer Are Not Automatic in Multi-Human Multi-Unmanned Aerial Vehicle Teams
items.abstract: ObjectiveThis study examined trust contagion and trust transfer in co-located multi-human multi-Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) teams and adopted the Actor-Partner Interdependence Model (APIM) to model trust dynamics in human-autonomy teams (HAT).BackgroundMost HAT research has focused on dyadic relationships, yet real-world operations increasingly involve multiple human operators collaborating with multiple agents. How trust spreads between human teammates and transfers across agents in non-dyadic contexts remains poorly understood.MethodA 3 (UAV reliability: High-High, Mixed, Low-Low; within-subjects) × 2 (Priming: Trust vs. Distrust; between-subjects) mixed design was used. Fifty-three dyads (N = 106) performed a target acquisition task in two-human, two-UAV teams. Subjective trust was analyzed using linear mixed models as the primary analysis, with APIM as a secondary exploratory analysis of dyadic influence.ResultsFor trust contagion, UAV reliability was the primary driver of trust, with no evidence that primed attitudes spread between operators, suggesting boundary conditions on when contagion occurs. For trust transfer, trust in the reliable UAV did not decline when paired with an unreliable one, supporting component-specific trust. Exploratory APIM helped disentangle dyadic interdependence and generate hypotheses for future work.ConclusionTrust in multi-human multi-agent teams was driven primarily by system reliability, with operators adopting component-specific trust, calibrating trust to each UAV individually.ApplicationSupporting calibrated trust depends first on system reliability and on direct experience with each agent's performance. APIM offers a means to distinguish an operator's own trust development from a teammate's influence, making it suited to studying trust in multi-human multi-agent teams.

items.abstract: This study develops and tests an integrated model that draws on selected constructs from the Technology Acceptance Model 3 (TAM3) and the Theory 10 of Planned Behavior (TPB) and incorporates artificial intelligence (AI) literacy to explain early childhood education (ECE) educators’ behavioral intention to use AI. Using partial least squares structural equation modeling to analyze survey data from 1,696 Chinese ECE educators (97.9% female), who were recruited primarily from the public sector, the integrated model accounted 15 for 89.2% of the variance in behavioral intention. Research Findings: AI literacy emerged as the most influential factor, demonstrating strong effects on perceived ease of use (PEOU), attitude, and perceived usefulness. Attitude was the strongest direct predictor of behavioral intention. AI anxiety showed limited influence, failing to affect PEOU. Theoretically, the integrated model offers a coherent 20 framework for understanding Chinese ECE educators’ intentions to adopt AI at work. items.title: Understanding user agency and structural conditions in information system implementation: a study in industrial maintenance
items.abstract: Purpose Users within the same organization may enact the same digital information system differently, creating diverse requirements and challenges for implementation. It is essential to view information system implementation as a process shaped by individuals' capacity to act within organizational structures, that is, through their agency. This study explores the manifestation of user agency and its associated structural conditions in information system implementation. Design/methodology/approach We examined users' experiences of information system implementation in two industrial companies' maintenance operations, through an interpretive qualitative study based on semi-structured interviews. Findings The study identifies four types of agency, namely eligible, estranged, skilled and motivated, and shows ways in which structural conditions of work design, social relationships and practices and situated individual resources in information system users' work both enable and hinder user's capacity to act during information system implementation. Practical implications The identified agency types can help managers in tailoring information system implementation support. Acknowledging work design, collaborative practices and situated resources enhances users' capacity to act with the new system. Originality/value This study contributes by introducing a typology of user agency in information system implementation: it provides a fine-grained lens to explain why users facing the same information system enact it differently and extends enactment-oriented information system research on human agency. Showing how agency is conditioned by work design, social relationships and practices and situated individual resources in users' unique work conditions, it addresses agency as part of the social and structural dynamics of information system implementation.

items.title: Unpacking “Personal” Health Informatics for Proactive Collective Care
items.abstract: Care is primarily a collective phenomenon, with a practice that involves sharing health and wellbeing information within a trusted “care circle” of family members and companions for sensemaking, interpretation, decision-making, and follow-through. However, current digital health tools and information systems are designed for individuals and primarily intended for Personal Health Informatics (PHI). This mismatch between collective practice and individualistic design creates new challenges for the proactive use of such systems in care settings and limits adoption, sustained engagement, and meaningful use. To examine how people practice collective care and how (if) they perceive, adopt, and integrate PHI systems for proactive care, we conducted a sequential mixed-methods study. Through an initial survey (n=87) and semi-structured interviews (n=22), we found that their practices involve collectively understanding, analyzing, and sensemaking health information. However, we also found that their use of existing systems to support such practices is constrained by factors at personal, relational, technological, and structural levels that evolve over time. To address these constraints and explore redesigning PHI toward “Collective Health Informatics”, we conducted eight stakeholder interview sessions with 12 participants, a follow-up survey (n=114), and six co-design workshops with 12 participants to understand the dynamics required in collective settings while retaining agency. Using a design probe evaluation (n=38), we refine a design vision for coordinated, trustworthy action across such care relationships. Our findings motivate CC-Proact, an operational map that translates ecological influences into three design levers: Agency, Elicitation, and Engagement. Using this map, our work empirically examines collective care practices and offers six design recommendations to build responsible systems that proactively support collective care.

items.title: What's the Difference? Voice Design and Confirmation Bias in AI-Assisted Self-Diagnosis: Anthropomorphic vs. Machine-Like Voice Output
items.abstract: As symptom checkers based on artificial intelligence (AI) are becoming common entry points for health information, their influence on lay users' diagnostic decisions raises questions about trust and bias. Of particular concern is confirmation bias, the tendency to favour information that supports one's existing belief while discounting information that contradicts it. One of the central design choices for such systems is the style of voice: whether they should present themselves with a human-like (anthropomorphic) or a clearly machine-like (xenomorphic) voice. This study investigates whether the voice design of an AI symptom checker modulates confirmation bias in self-diagnosis. In a within-subjects online experiment (N = 81 participants, 648 trials), participants selected a diagnosis and rated their confidence, then heard an AI-generated recommendation that either confirmed or contradicted their initial choice, delivered by an anthropomorphic or a machine-like voice, before deciding again. We observed a strong, direction-dependent influence of the AI: participants revised their diagnosis in 45.7% of trials when the AI contradicted them versus 1.2% when it confirmed them (generalised linear mixed model, GLMM, p < .001); confidence rose under confirmation but barely moved under contradiction (robust linear mixed model, p < .001); and decisions took longer after contradiction (Gamma GLMM, p < .001). This effect did not differ between the two voices (no voice or interaction term was significant, smallest p = .282), even though a manipulation check confirmed the voices were perceived as markedly different. The findings suggest that the direction of an AI recommendation, rather than the anthropomorphism of its voice, drives confirmation-related bias in AI-assisted self-diagnosis.

items.title: When Does an Answer Become Enough? Evidence, Understanding, and Inquiry in AI-Mediated Research
items.abstract: Generative AI systems increasingly mediate how researchers encounter and make sense of scholarly information. By producing coherent explanations from multiple sources, these systems may influence how users assess their understanding, evaluate supporting evidence, and decide whether further investigation is necessary. This project investigates how AI-generated scholarly synthesis shapes judgments of explanatory and evidentiary sufficiency in academic research. Its central question is whether, and under what conditions, the perceived completeness of an explanation influences a researcher’s assessment of the evidence supporting it and their decision to continue or conclude an information search. The research draws on library and information science, human-computer interaction, epistemology, and cognitive psychology. It examines established accounts of information satisficing, search stopping behavior, cognitive authority, epistemic dependence, and metacognitive calibration to assess how these concepts explain information-seeking decisions in AI-mediated environments. A central distinction concerns the difference between understanding an explanation and having sufficient grounds to accept its claims. These judgments may coincide, but they need not. An explanation may adequately address a research question while leaving important uncertainties about source quality, methodological limitations, or competing interpretations unresolved. Conversely, reliance on a well-supported synthesis may be entirely justified without extensive examination of every underlying source. Rather than treating reduced information seeking as an inherent failure, the project considers how researchers determine when further inquiry is warranted. It examines the conditions under which AI-generated synthesis may support well-calibrated judgments, encourage critical engagement with evidence, or contribute to premature conclusions. The project aims to develop a theoretically grounded account of evidentiary judgment and inquiry termination in AI-mediated scholarly research, with implications for information literacy, scholarly information practices, and the design of research support systems.

items.title: When meaningful work becomes inaccessible: Disability, ableism and passive agency
items.abstract: Why does meaningful work become inaccessible to certain groups? Existing literature increasingly recognizes that access to meaningful work is shaped by both subjective experiences and objective conditions, yet it remains less clear about how and why such access becomes systematically constrained. In particular, prior studies tend to foreground workers’ active agency in engaging with, negotiating or resisting these conditions of meaningful work, but they offer limited insight into how this capacity itself may be restricted. Drawing on Archer’s distinction between active and passive agency, we conceptualize passive agency as a mechanism through which structural constraints limit workers’ capability for purposive action. Based on 33 interviews with disabled workers in China, we show how ableism acts as a structural constraint, positioning disabled workers as passive agents, restricting their capacity to experience work as meaningful by limiting opportunities for autonomy, dignity and recognition. In doing so, we extend current understanding of meaningful work by specifying how structural constraints give rise to passive agency, thereby systematically foreclosing access to meaningful work. We also clarify contingent conditions under which more active forms of agency may be enacted, and thus meaningful work can be sustained.

items.title: When Principles Compound: Lessons Learned from Implementing Best Practices in Ethical Dataset Curation
items.abstract: Scholars have proposed ethical principles and frameworks to support industry practitioners developing responsible AI. To enable these from theory to practice, a subset of research explores how practitioners actually enact abstract ethical concepts and guidance, surfacing factors that limit their efforts—e.g., organizational support—and informing ways to strengthen efforts towards safe and ethical AI in practice—e.g., practical checklists, educational workbooks. Curiously, this has been underexplored in relation to practitioners curating ethical datasets, the very foundation needed for fair ML technologies, despite the existence of various data ethics principles. It is unsurprising, then, that reports continue to emerge of ML datasets curated through questionable practices, including non-consensual web-scraping and exploitative labor practices. To address this gap, we describe the experiences of a project team curating FHIBE: a fair, human-centric benchmark dataset for computer vision technologies, grounded in recommendations by data ethics and fair ML scholars. Using an ethnographic lens, we share the team’s motivation and the set of principles FHIBE was based on, the challenges team members faced trying to execute multiple principles at once, and the ways they adapted in lieu of resources or insights from preceding scholarship. By tracing one team’s end-to-end data curation efforts, we offer new insights into practitioners’ realities translating data ethics, to inform valuable avenues for HCI and policy researchers to address in the future.

items.title: When the Strands Disagree: Using Divergence in Mixed-Methods Joint Displays to Refine Practical Frameworks
items.abstract: Joint displays, which set quantitative and qualitative findings side by side, have become a standard device for integrating results in mixed-methods research. In practice, researchers tend to report convergence and to explain away divergence by attributing it to a weakness in one strand. This methodological paper argues that divergence is frequently the most informative product of a joint display and shows how it can be used to refine a practical framework. The argument is developed through a worked example from a mixed-methods study of expatriate educator retention in international high schools in Guangzhou, China, in which a survey of 52 educators was integrated with written interviews with 11. Ten domains were classified as convergent, complementary, divergent or qualitative only: five converged, three were complementary, one diverged and one emerged only in the interviews.

items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is rapidly reshaping higher education, yet many students still use AI at a basic level and lack a systematic approach to designing learning games in collaboration with AI. This study, the first phase of a research and development (R&D) project, aimed 1) to examine the current conditions and priority developmental needs regarding AI literacy and game design skills among higher education students, and 2) to synthesize a design framework for human–AI collaborative game-based learning innovation. A survey was combined with bibliometric mapping and content synthesis. The survey sample comprised 78 undergraduate students in Computer Education, selected through purposive sampling from a population of 128 students; the document dataset consisted of 31 publications retrieved from Scopus and OpenAlex after deduplication. Survey data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, and instrument reliability was acceptable (Cronbach’s a = 0.89). Document data were analyzed through bibliometric mapping and content synthesis using bibliometrix (R) and VOSviewer. The findings indicated that students’ AI literacy (M = 3.09, SD = 0.83) and game design skills (M = 2.95, SD = 0.90) were at a moderate level, while developmental needs were high (M = 4.14, SD = 0.62), particularly for a systematic AI-supported design approach (M = 4.21, SD = 0.58). The synthesis yielded a six-component design framework covering learner-experience-first design, AI role definition, iterative evidence-based design, MDA mapping, ethical reflection, and prompt preparation. The framework offers an empirical basis for designing learning innovation that integrates AI literacy, game design, and responsible human–AI collaboration, and it guides the development phase of the project.

items.title: “I check it when it feels wrong” – Computer Science Student Usage and Perspectives on AI Chatbots
items.abstract: We present a qualitative interview study with 17 Canadian computer science and software engineering undergraduates exploring their self-initiated, unsupervised AI chatbot use. We find that most participants, despite being CS students often assumed to have stronger technical intuitions, lacked an accurate understanding of how generative AI produces output. This miscalibration was associated with plausibility-based fact-checking: participants who described genAI as a retrieval or database system had no reliable trigger for verifying confidently-stated misinformation. We discuss implications for AI literacy education and human-AI interaction design.

items.title: A Protective Agent Architecture for the Last Human Step: Influence Without Authority, from Web Pages to Agent Approvals
items.abstract: When an AI agent proposes an action, the user’s decision may be reduced to a brief approval step. A misleading summary can obscure consequences at that point. We propose a protective agent architecture for web browsing and agent approvals intended to inform the user’s decision without exercising authority over it. The design combines on-device estimates of behavioral deviation with deterministic intervention rules specified by the user in advance. Interventions would preserve existing choices while adjusting visual emphasis, exposing omitted information, and adding options. For agent approvals, an independent channel would compare the request with the proposed action’s tool-call arguments. A web-browsing prototype is available; the approval layer and empirical evaluation remain future work. We describe its mechanisms, an illustrative approval scenario, and an evaluation plan, including the unresolved relationship between behavioral deviation and supervisory bandwidth.

items.title: AI Reliance in the Fantasy American Football Lineup-Setting Task
items.abstract: Analysts, athletes and coaches have long relied upon decision support tools, but new AI capabilities raise questions of whether they can “appropriately rely” on these models. In this work, we explore the starting lineup decisions of fantasy American football managers in the presence of projected points. Across more than 2.5 million lineup-weeks from a single fantasy platform during the 2025 NFL season, we find that fantasy managers’ starting lineups appropriately rely on AI advice in only 15.8% to 26.8% of cases. Despite managers’ observed near complete reliance, limited deviation from AI advice is often harmful to their decision-making. Bridging literature from critical data studies and AI reliance, we discuss possible explanations for this behavior, and offer design directions towards complementarity in this setting. Finally, we highlight tensions revealed by the case of fantasy football, and invite researchers to consider SportsHCI as a site to bridge social desirability and technical possibility in and beyond sports.

items.title: Autonomy of Boundedly Rational Agents in Dyadic Interactions
items.abstract: AI agents now work alongside people in domains ranging from autonomous vehicles to conversational systems. A recurring question is when an agent’s behavior counts as self-determined rather than merely reactive to its human partner. This matters for ethical conduct, which is widely argued to require some form of autonomy. Yet, its computational meaning is rarely made precise. In this paper, we study an agent’s autonomy in dyadic interactions, measured by the extent to which the agent’s behavior is explained by its own state rather than by its partner’s signals. This quantity captures information-theoretic self-determination as inferred from interaction traces. We characterize autonomy as a function of how deterministically the agent acts, how strongly it optimizes payoffs, and how much past interaction it retains. Using analytical and numerical results from four distinct games, we find that autonomy peaks at high but sub-maximal determinism and is dissociable from rationality. All four settings achieve the same level of autonomy regardless of the agent’s payoff disposition, so rationality never raises the ceiling. What the payoff structure determines is the direction in which rationality trades against determinism. Payoff-seeking play economizes on determinism in one setting, payoff-avoiding play in another, and neither matters where the agent cannot influence its payoff. Our results suggest design principles for interactive agents that remain consistent and self-determined.

items.title: Beyond Automation: Exploring Employees’ Perceptions of Artificial Intelligence, Job Insecurity, and Workplace Identity in The Modern Workplace
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has become a part of every organisation's day-to-day operations and is a factor in the way work is being assigned, done, directed and checked. Discussions about this change have primarily been around automation, efficiency and jobs, but also about how an employee's sense of security, competence in their role, independence and sense of identity at work is affected by AI. In this article, we delve into the interconnections between employees' attitudes toward AI, their feelings of job insecurity, and workplace identity. The five interrelated themes were: (1) Ambivalence about the use of AI: some experiences it as a tool to augment their work while others worry about being monitored, deskilled, and displaced; (2) Anticipatory fear of loss: fear of job loss can occur even if the number of jobs does not decrease; (3) Remediated and reinforced professional identity: when AI is used to complement their job, it enhances their sense of competence, while when it digitises their core job, it threatens it; (4) Algorithmic management reconfigures autonomy: when automating parts of their job, employees' autonomy is reassigned, while when parts of their job are kept by humans and coded into algorithms, they lose some autonomy; (5) Algorithmic management experiences depend on the organizational support, the transparency of communication, participation, and reskilling. From a theoretical perspective, the study synthesizes the concepts of job insecurity, social and/or organizational identification, technology acceptance and resistance, sociotechnical systems and human capital, and is able to articulate a framework beyond the deterministic replacement stories. The reality is that HR teams and leaders need to approach the integration of AI as a transformational journey rather than simply a technological fix, and have to do so. It concludes by proposing that although the technical difficulty is a consideration, a more important one is how well staff can feel secure, competent and valued as professionals in the context of the integration of AI.

items.title: BIM Adoption and the Industry-Academia Digital Gap in Ecuador: A TOE-TAM Assessment
items.abstract: BIM adoption in non-mandated emerging economies is a complex sociotechnical process where organizational culture, institutional frameworks, and cognitive dynamics interact. Current literature remains fragmented, evaluating macro-level organizational maturity or micro-level student technology acceptance in isolation, thereby lacking an integrative framework to model how structural governance conditions individual acceptance and perpetuates the digital gap. Addressing this theoretical gap, this study operationalizes an integrated Technology Organization Environment (TOE) and Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) framework. Using non-parametric inferential analysis across AECO organizations (n = 74) and academic-professional stakeholders (n = 71) in Ecuador, findings reveal that despite basic 3D adoption (68.92%), severe governance deficits persist: 51.35% lack defined BIM roles, 66.22% lack training plans, and only 17.57% utilize ISO 19650-compliant Common Data Environments (CDE). High Perceived Usefulness (PU = 62.86%) and learning intention (BIU = 94.20%) are constrained by low Perceived Ease of Use (PEOU), tied to a 58.57% 2D CAD reliance. Inferential testing confirmed macro-organizational factors drive individual acceptance (p < 0.01) and revealed a significant inverse alignment between market demands and learning outcomes (rs = −0.62, p < 0.001). Beyond practical Project-Based Learning (PBL) applications, this study’s primary theoretical contribution establishes a validated baseline identifying PEOU as the core cognitive-operational bottleneck during technological transitions.

items.title: Can Human Verification Restore Felt Responsibility for AI-Assisted Knowledge Work?
items.abstract: Generative AI (genAI) co-produces the work of hundreds of millions of people. Humanoversight, the default safeguard in AI governance, assumes that people still feel responsiblefor the outputs they approve. Yet genAI assistance can lower psychological ownership ofsuch outputs, and whether the resulting loss of felt responsibility can be repaired remainsunclear. Drawing on the triangle model of responsibility and psychological ownership theory,we propose that psychological ownership is how people experience the causal link betweenthemselves and an outcome, that genAI assistance weakens this link, and that a mandatoryverification step after generation can rebuild it. We derive five hypotheses on the erosion andrestoration of psychological ownership and felt responsibility and on revision after criticism,and we outline a 3 × 2 experiment to test them.

items.title: Communication Characteristics and Needs: Effects of Transferring Decision-making Level from Humans to AI Advisors in Academia
items.abstract: Academic advisors increasingly face heavy workloads driven by rising student demand. Designing AI-driven administrative systems based on users’ needs can help alleviate this burden. Our study examines how the perception of human needs and characteristics of communication are affected when AI systems replace human advisors in academic settings. This study employed a mixed-methods design with semi-structured interviews (N = 31) and pre-post surveys (N = 119) to investigate user needs and validate findings for an academic agent-based support system. Our findings show a selective pattern: shifting to AI agents produced significant declines in competence, relatedness, and impactfulness, while autonomy, engagement, and security showed no detected difference. Human advisors were valued for empathy and contextual judgment in complex decisions, whereas AI agents were valued for availability, efficiency, and emotional consistency. Rather than competing alternatives, these results point toward complementary systems that position agents as first-line support while preserving human connection for high-stakes, emotionally complex interactions.

items.title: Continuance Use Intention of Generative AI Use among Higher Education Students: A Systematic Literature Review Based on the Extended ECM-ISC
items.abstract: While initial adoption marks the preliminary phase of Generative AI integration in higher education, long-term impact on learning relies heavily on students’ continuance intention. This Systematic Literature Review (SLR) investigates publication trajectories, theoretical frameworks, and contextual determinants to extend the Expectation Confirmation Model of Information Systems Continuance (ECM-ISC) within tertiary education. Following structured planning, execution, and reporting phases, a comprehensive search across Scopus, IEEE, and PubMed databases spanning 2021 to 2026 yielded 2,107 initial records, from which 31 peer-reviewed papers met strict eligibility and quality criteria. The analysis reveals an exponential rise in GenAI continuance research during 2025 and 2026. The theoretical frameworks commonly employed include TAM, ECM/ECT, UTAUT/UTAUT2, TTF, D&M IS Success Model, S-O-R, and hybrid SEM-ANN approaches. The main findings indicate that perceived information quality, trust, perceived risk, and intrinsic motivation are relevant external factors for extending ECM-ISC. Synthesizing these dimensions, this study delivers a refined ECM-ISC framework tailored to higher education, offering strategic insights for GenAI system design and institutional policymaking.

items.title: Del tutor mecánico al tutor generativo: inteligencia artificial en la educación y sus efectos en la salud cognitiva, mental y emocional de los estudiantes. Revisión integrativa (1955-2026)
items.abstract: Objetivo. Sintetizar la evidencia sobre la inteligencia artificial (IA) en la educación, desde el origen del término (1955) hasta 2026, y analizar sus efectos en la salud cognitiva, mental y emocional de estudiantes y docentes, por nivel formativo.Método. Revisión integrativa según Whittemore y Knafl. Búsqueda sistematizada en PubMed el 27 de septiembre de 2026 (934 registros; 93 revisiones), complementada con búsqueda dirigida en arXiv, ACM, Nature, PNAS y literatura institucional, y rastreo de citas. Se incluyeron 23 fuentes empíricas o de síntesis y 14 documentos normativos e institucionales, jerarquizados por nivel de evidencia y analizados mediante síntesis temática y cuantitativa descriptiva.Resultados. El efecto de la IA depende del diseño pedagógico. Tutores con andamiaje produjeron ganancias de 0,23 a 0,31 desviaciones estándar (DE) en Nigeria y mayor aprendizaje en física universitaria. El acceso libre a GPT-4 redujo el desempeño 17 % al retirarlo. En lo cognitivo, la descarga cognitiva se asocia con menor pensamiento crítico y menor conectividad neural en escritura asistida (evidencia preliminar). En lo mental, la dependencia de IA generativa se asocia con ansiedad, depresión y agotamiento académico, mediados por menor autoeficacia. El uso diario intensivo de chatbots se asocia con soledad y dependencia emocional. Los chatbots basados en terapia cognitivo-conductual y las simulaciones clínicas muestran beneficios. La evidencia es escasa en formación técnica, tecnológica y de posgrado.Conclusiones. La IA funciona como andamio o como muleta según el diseño que la rodea. Se propone el Modelo de Andamiaje Protector y recomendaciones para la educación abierta y a distancia.

items.title: Delegating or Doing? Understanding User Behavior in Hybrid Human–Agent Interfaces
items.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly embedded into applications, allowing users to complete tasks either through direct manipulation or by delegating actions to conversational agents. However, little is known about how users balance these modalities when both are available. We present a web-based content management system augmented with an LLM agent through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), enabling users to perform CRUD tasks through a graphical interface, a conversational agent, or both. We conducted a between-subjects study (N=73) comparing three interaction modes: Traditional-Only, AI-First, and Hybrid. Across sixteen scenarios, we analyzed task completion time, interaction logs, and delegation behavior. AI-assisted interaction significantly reduced clicks, page navigations, and scrolling, indicating lower interaction effort. Surprisingly, these reductions did not translate into faster task completion, as task duration did not differ significantly across conditions. We also found no significant relationship between CRUD operation type and delegation, suggesting that users did not systematically avoid delegating higher-risk actions. Instead, delegation varied far more between participants than between tasks, with individual differences accounting for roughly half the variance in assistant use (ICC =.50). Our findings suggest that the primary benefit of human–agent interfaces may be reducing interaction effort rather than improving speed, and that delegation reflects who the user is more than what the task demands.

items.title: Drivers of Student Interest and Attitudes in STEM
items.abstract: Purpose: This study investigated the factors that predict senior high school students' interest in and attitudes toward Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics (STEM) education in Ghana. It examined how intrinsic motivation, self-determination, self-efficacy, career motivation, and grade motivation were linked to students' emotional engagement in STEM learning. Design/Methodology/Approach: This quantitative cross-sectional study used a structured questionnaire measured on a five-point Likert scale to collect data from 767 students. Students in Forms 1 to 3 were selected through proportional stratified sampling at three purposively selected senior high schools in the Greater Accra Region. Multiple regression analysis was used to identify the motivational factors that predict students’ interest in and attitude toward STEM. Research Limitation: This study is limited by its cross-sectional design, which restricts the ability to draw causal inferences. It also relied on self-reported data from students in one region of Ghana, which might limit its generalisability. Findings: The analysis showed that intrinsic motivation and self-determination strongly predict both STEM interest and attitudes. Self-efficacy and career motivation also predicted STEM interest but did not significantly predict attitude. In contrast, grade motivation predicts attitudes but not interest. The findings indicate that intrinsic motivation and self-determination are consistently associated with both STEM interest and STEM attitude, while other motivational factors show outcome-specific patterns. Practical Implication: The results suggest the need for educational changes that support student autonomy, promote inquiry-based learning, and improve career counselling. These changes can help connect teaching methods with motivational factors that maintain students’ interest and positive attitudes toward STEM. Social Implication: By highlighting the key psychological factors that drive STEM engagement, this study provides insights for policymakers looking to improve low STEM participation rates and encourage long-term economic development through more scientifically informed and skilled youth. Originality/Value: The findings indicate that STEM interest and attitudes reflect distinct motivational patterns. Intrinsic motivation and self-determination predict students’ STEM interest and STEM attitude, while self-efficacy and career motivation predict interest, and grade motivation predicts attitudes. It extends context-specific evidence and supports differentiated interpretations of STEM motivation.

items.title: Du conseil social à la réassurance algorithmique : IA, intimité et hésitation décisionnelle dans les cultures numériques marocaines, africaines et arabes
items.abstract: Des utilisateurs soumettent désormais aux IA conversationnelles des conflits relationnels, des hésitations morales ou des décisions personnelles pour obtenir une validation avant d’agir. Cet article conceptualise comme réassurance algorithmique le recours à l’IA pour sortir de l’hésitation décisionnelle, état où l’information suffirait à décider mais où le sentiment de suffisance fait défaut. À partir d’une revue intégrative ciblée, nous soutenons que l’enjeu distinctif n’est pas la recherche de réassurance elle-même, mais une architecture de service qui la rend disponible, privée et presque sans friction sociale. Nous développons le mécanisme de délégation de la clôture décisionnelle : ce qui se déplace n’est pas la décision, mais le signal que la délibération peut s’arrêter. Le caractère intime de la demande explique en partie que la consultation se répète sans gain informationnel. Dans certains des contextes marocains, africains et arabes documentés ici, le conseil peut s’inscrire dans des relations peu substituables ; nous traitons cette configuration comme une variable à mesurer, non comme un trait culturel. Les propositions, non testées, sont assorties d’un agenda empirique et d’implications pour la conception des services conversationnels et la gouvernance des données intimes.

items.title: Employee Wellness Programmes in Manufacturing: A Critical Review of Causal Evidence, Productivity Outcomes and Job Satisfaction
items.abstract: Wellness programs for employees are becoming essential in manufacturing since occupational health, work organization, physical demands, and psychosocial conditions can affect worker wellness and functional performance. This paper reviews the impact of programmes which enhance health in the workplace on productivity and job satisfaction in a manufacturing setting. A systematic critical assessment was conducted of peer-reviewed intervention studies, systematic reviews and authoritative occupational-health advice related specifically to Covid-19 pandemic and literature from 2020-2026 including relevant earlier studies. The existing body of research deals with both the promotion of physical health and risk management and stress management approaches. Programs that improve health behaviours, perceived wellbeing, work ability and other aspects of employee experience can be effective, according to the research. Nonetheless, the proof pertaining to absenteeism, objectively assessed output, and job satisfaction consistently shows improvement. The differences in study design, participant selection, duration of programme, measurement of outcome and context of industry prohibits direct comparisons and causality interpretation. The findings revealed that integrating individual support with risk mitigation can enhance the efficacy of wellness programs for manufacturing employees. In addition, supportive supervision, employee involvement, and execution consistent with shift schedules and production requirements are also favorable. The research also reveals that self-reported productivity as a proxy for verified production cannot address limitation and there are not enough rigorous longitudinal studies in manufacturing. Future studies should combine established job-satisfaction measurement instruments with objectively recorded measurement of output, quality, absence, and safety indicators, while also exploring programme costs, equity of access, and longer-term sustainability.

items.title: Foundation Pareto Flow Policy for Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning
items.abstract: The overarching goal of reinforcement learning (RL) is to efficiently optimize the agent's policy for various environments, tasks, dynamics, and even user preferences, which often consist of multiple and potentially conflicting rewards/objectives. This necessitates the learning of Pareto-optimal policies that can navigate different trade-offs among objectives. However, existing multi-objective RL (MORL) methods, whether trained online or offline, are typically limited to task- or objective-specific policy learning and do not address generalization of learned trade-offs to unseen tasks/objectives. In this work, we propose the Foundation Pareto Flow Policy (FP2) for offline MORL in continuous robotic control, inspired by the pre-mid-post-training paradigm underlying recent foundation models. Specifically, we instantiate FP2 as a multi-modal diffusion transformer equipped with a likelihood-free flow matching loss, enabling unified, scalable, and instructable learning of diverse trade-off trajectories. We further develop a three-stage training pipeline to gradually optimize the policy: (1) pre-training on a large-scale MORL dataset, (2) mid-training on a carefully curated high-quality dataset, and (3) post-training on few collected trajectory data from new tasks and trade-offs. Empirical results demonstrate that FP2 outperforms previous state-of-the-art methods on most tasks of the D4MORL benchmark, achieving superior zero-shot interpolation and extrapolation on complex Pareto manifolds as well as efficient few-shot adaptation of the learned trade-off prior to new continuous-control tasks. Code is available at https://github.com/FibonacciRabbit/FP2.

items.title: From Perceived Trust to Delegation in Agentic AI: Reliability, Apparent Bistability, and Delegation Thresholds
items.abstract: Trust is central to human–agent interaction, but agentic AI raises a stronger question: when does perceived trust translate into delegated action? This poster introduces an agent-based simulation in which agents delegate when trust exceeds a threshold, observe success or failure, and update trust through outcome feedback with tunable failure sensitivity. We vary AI reliability and delegation thresholds while examining social conformity and failure sensitivity. Results show that unreliable systems drive abandonment, while intermediate regimes can produce apparent bistability: identical AI reliability can lead to adoption or rejection depending on initial trust and the delegation threshold. Conformity can sustain delegation by preventing isolated trust collapse. These findings suggest that delegation thresholds act as control parameters for sustained reliance. Future work will validate the model with human participants and heterogeneous agent profiles and tasks.

items.title: From Tool to Agent: How Worker Needs Reorganize Across the Agentic Roles of Workplace AI
items.abstract: As AI systems gain agency in workplaces, workers increasingly interact with systems that do more than support tasks: they make decisions, allocate work, and shape how workers communicate with others. We interviewed 16 workers in healthcare, finance, and management about their daily interactions with workplace AI systems. Across these domains, AI occupied three agentic roles: assistant, supporting worker decision-making; arbiter, making consequential decisions that workers had to explain to downstream stakeholders; and manager, directing work and displacing social structures through which work had been negotiated and learned. We find that worker needs depended on how decision authority and accountability were configured around the AI system. Explanation, control, accountability, and communication each took different meanings depending on whether AI supported, decided, or directed work. We contribute a role-based account of workplace human-agent interaction and identify accountability-authority asymmetry as a mechanism through which AI deployments can place responsibility on workers for outcomes whose authority has shifted to AI. We discuss implications for designing workplace AI around both the agent and its surrounding agency configuration.

items.title: From Tutor to Listener: Exploring Backchannel Modality in Embodied AI for Think-Aloud Learning
items.abstract: Generative AI can support learning, but it may also encourage cognitive outsourcing by replacing learners’ own thinking. This study reframes AI from an information provider to a responsive listener that promotes cognitive engagement and self-explanation. We introduce Hearble, a minimal robotic listener designed to isolate the effects of different backchannel modalities. Using a between-subjects design, we compare four conditions: no response, visual, nonverbal acoustic, and verbal backchannels. We examine how these conditions affect utterance elaboration, cognitive load, immediate comprehension, knowledge transfer, and perceived agency. Rather than limiting AI intervention to preserving learners’ cognitive processes, we investigate whether AI can actively support them by encouraging learners to articulate and elaborate their own thoughts. This work presents the physical AI listener as an alternative interaction paradigm for learning and provides a controlled foundation for future research on how embodiment, facial expressions, gestures, and other audience cues shape learning and agency.

items.title: How AI Agent Memory and Personality Reshape Trust Calibration in Human-Agent Collaboration
items.abstract: AI agents increasingly remember prior interactions and present themselves through distinct personalities. Whether these relational features help users calibrate their trust appropriately, or instead impose hidden costs without improving how well they rely on agent guidance, is an open and consequential design question. In a remote virtual reality study (N = 92), we independently varied whether an agent referenced its shared history with the user and whether its personality matched the user’s own style. Agents that made memory references caused users to slow down and deliberate longer at every decision point, yet this caution produced no improvement in compliance quality—a pattern we call the memory paradox. More social did not mean better calibrated. Personality congruence did not make users trust the agent more overall, but it did make their trust judgments more behaviorally coherent. Across all conditions, participants followed incorrect agent guidance at a strikingly high rate, and no relational design feature reduced this automation bias. Taken together, these findings argue that the core challenge in human-agent collaboration is not building trust, but calibrating it: AI agents should be evaluated by how accurately users rely on them, not by how humanlike they feel.

items.title: Human Oversight in Agentic AI: Explainability, Anthropomorphism, and the Boundary of Cognitive Forcing
items.abstract: Explainability helps users assess evidence behind an AI recommendation, but it may not change decisions when that evidence goes unexamined. The problem is sharper in agentic decision support, where one assistant interprets evidence, explains its assessment, and recommends an action, while anthropomorphic delivery may add social credibility. Cognitive forcing, operationalised here as Human Intervention Checkpoints (HICs), requires users to specify what the assistant should examine before it recommends. We report a randomised 2 × 2 × 2 hiring experiment (N = 211) in which recruiters assessed a candidate whose unmet role-critical requirements were stated in every recommendation. Advancement was not associated with explanatory provenance, anthropomorphic delivery, HIC presence, or opening source documents. Post-task perceived explainability was associated with perceived anthropomorphism and trust, and trust was associated with advancement. In HIC-present conditions, 70 participants directed the assistant to a role-critical requirement and received Hold, yet 46 advanced. The findings identify a boundary of cognitive forcing: influence over what the agent evaluated and recommended did not reliably carry through to the final human decision.

items.title: Implementing a Humanistic Approach in Akidah Akhlak Learning to Cultivate Students’ Love of Science at MAN 2 Klaten
items.abstract: Objective: This study describes how an Akidah Akhlak teacher applies a humanistic approach at State Islamic Senior High School (Madrasah Aliyah Negeri, MAN) 2 Klaten, Indonesia, and interprets how these practices may support the conditions for students’ love of science. Theoretical framework: The analysis draws on Maslow’s hierarchy of needs, Rogers’ person-centred learning, Freire’s dialogical education and Deci and Ryan’s self-determination theory, and treats hubb al-ʿilm as an Islamic educational orientation that overlaps with, but is not identical to, intrinsic motivation. Literature review: The literature review examines humanistic Islamic education through Maslow, Rogers, Freire, and self-determination theory, highlighting the relationship between student autonomy, emotional needs, moral learning, and hubb al-ʿilm. Research gap: Earlier studies of humanistic Akidah Akhlak learning have mostly examined primary-level madrasahs and moral outcomes such as courtesy and discipline, leaving field evidence on knowledge-oriented outcomes at the Madrasah Aliyah level limited. Methods: A qualitative case study used semi-structured interviews, passive participatory classroom observation and documentation review. Data were analyzed with the interactive model of Miles, Huberman and Saldaña, and credibility was supported by source triangulation and member checking. Results: Three interrelated strategies emerged: differentiating methods according to class conduciveness; negotiating relational agreements that recognize students’ basic needs and autonomy, namely a responsibility-based eating and drinking policy and the absence of homework; and responding to mistakes with mild consequences followed by reflective dialogue on the purpose of seeking knowledge. Together, these practices appear to create a low-threat climate that is conducive to curiosity and to a shift from external towards more internalized motivation. Because the evidence rests mainly on the teacher’s account, supported by classroom observation and documents, the study does not claim that students’ love of science was measured or has increased. Implications: The three-stage model offered here is a contextual interpretation of one case, and may inform teacher reflection and training in comparable madrasahs. Novelty: The study foregrounds hubb al-ʿilm as an affective orientation in humanistic Akidah Akhlak learning at the Madrasah Aliyah level and documents concrete relational agreements that are rarely reported.
